children.title: Decision-Role Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Strategic, assignment, sequencing, timing, and recourse decision blocks.

assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite decision-index set.
Each represented decision index is assigned exactly one declared architectural role.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I=I_M\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_S\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_L\).

notation.meaning: indices controlled by the integer-programming master
indices controlled by the constraint-processing submodel
indices serving a linking or communication role

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition of decision indices by their computational roles in a hybrid constraint–integer architecture.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a hybrid model have decision vector \(x=(x_i)_{i\in I}\). A decision-role partition is a family \((I_M,I_S,I_L)\) of pairwise disjoint subsets satisfying \(I=I_M\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_S\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_L\). Variables indexed by \(I_M\) are controlled by the integer-programming master, variables indexed by \(I_S\) are controlled by a constraint-processing submodel, and variables indexed by \(I_L\) occur in, or communicate values between, both components. Empty role classes are permitted. If one physical decision is represented by component-specific copies, the copies occupy their respective component-local classes, and an equality or channeling relation supplies the link; that relation is a constraint rather than a decision index.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision indices are partitioned into master, subproblem, and linking roles according to which hybrid component controls or communicates each decision; linking constraints between duplicated copies are not themselves decision indices.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Role Partitioning

children.title: Constraint-Family Partitioning
children.top_down_role: Linear, logical, global-constraint, and domain-specific constraint blocks.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Family Partitioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition of model constraints among integer, constraint-processing, and linking components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{c_j:j\in J\}\) be the constraints of a hybrid model. A constraint-family partition is a disjoint decomposition \(J=J_M\mathbin{\dot\cup}J_S\mathbin{\dot\cup}J_L\). Constraints indexed by \(J_M\) are enforced by the integer-programming component, those indexed by \(J_S\) are enforced by the constraint-processing component, and those indexed by \(J_L\) express cross-component activation, channeling, or consistency. The partition is representational: every original constraint has one owning component, while any additional linking constraints are explicitly indexed in \(J_L\). Equivalent reformulations may therefore induce different constraint-family partitions of the same feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint indices are divided into integer-programming, constraint-processing, and linking families, with each original constraint assigned one owner.
assumptions_latex: \(J\) is a finite index set for the represented model constraints.
Every original constraint has exactly one enforcing component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J=J_M\mathbin{\dot\cup}J_S\mathbin{\dot\cup}J_L\).

notation.meaning: constraints owned by the integer-programming component
constraints owned by the constraint-processing component

children.title: Partition Assignment Criteria
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria for assigning model components to CP, MIP, or shared treatment.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition Assignment Criteria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-formedness and locality conditions for assigning variables and constraints to hybrid components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For decision partition \((I_M,I_S,I_L)\), constraint partition \((J_M,J_S,J_L)\), and incidence sets \(N(j)\subseteq I\), an assignment is admissible when the partitions are disjoint and exhaustive and, for each \(k\in\{M,S\}\), \(j\in J_k\) implies \(N(j)\subseteq I_k\cup I_L\). Moreover, every \(j\in J_L\) must intersect at least two role classes or encode an explicit cross-component relation. Thus a component-owned constraint contains only locally controlled or linking decisions, while any relation coupling master-controlled and submodel-controlled decisions is assigned to the linking family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An admissible assignment is exhaustive, disjoint, locally closed under constraint incidence, and classifies every genuine cross-component relation as linking.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite index sets.
\(N(j)\) contains exactly the decision indices occurring in constraint \(j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(j\in J_k\Rightarrow N(j)\subseteq I_k\cup I_L\) for every \(k\in\{M,S\}\), with cross-role constraints assigned to \(J_L\).

notation.meaning: decision-index incidence set of constraint j

children.title: Cross-Component Variable Coupling
children.top_down_role: Common decisions, channeling relations, and projected information connecting model components.

children.title: Linking Relations
children.top_down_role: Channeling, implication, aggregation, and projection relations connecting model components.

knowledge_statements.title: Linking Relations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relations that couple component-local variable copies or decisions owned by different hybrid components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\in U\) and \(v\in V\) denote decisions owned by distinct components. A linking relation is a constraint \(R(u,v)\) whose feasible set \(L=\{(u,v)\in U\times V:R(u,v)\}\) restricts their joint values and cannot be expressed as a restriction on \(u\) alone or \(v\) alone. For duplicated representations of one decision, the canonical linking relation is equality, \(u=v\). More generally, linking may be functional, \(v=\phi(u)\), or relational, \((u,v)\in L\), provided it communicates the cross-component compatibility required by the original model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linking relation restricts decisions owned by different components; equality between duplicated variable copies is the canonical case.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(V\) are the domains of decisions owned by distinct components.
\(R\) is a well-defined predicate on \(U\times V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L=\{(u,v)\in U\times V:R(u,v)\}\) is a cross-component feasibility restriction.

notation.meaning: set of compatible cross-component value pairs
optional channeling map between component representations

children.title: Shared Variable Roles
children.top_down_role: Common decisions whose values or bounds are maintained across solver viewpoints.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared Variable Roles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of a decision whose value participates in multiple hybrid components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given component models with variable-index sets \(I_M\) and \(I_S\), a shared variable is a modeled decision \(z\) represented in both components, either by one common symbol or by copies \(z^M\) and \(z^S\). Its shared role requires every feasible hybrid assignment to satisfy \(z^M=z^S\), or an explicitly declared equivalent channel relation. A shared variable may transmit a master decision to the submodel, return a submodel-derived quantity to the master, or act bidirectionally; this communication direction is distinct from the mathematical requirement that both component representations denote one compatible decision.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared variable occurs in both components and must have one compatible value, even when represented by separate local copies.
assumptions_latex: The two component representations refer to the same modeled decision.
Each local copy has a declared domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z^M=z^S\), or a declared equivalent channel relation, holds in every feasible hybrid assignment.

notation.meaning: master-component copy of the shared decision
constraint-component copy of the shared decision

children.title: Cross-Component Consistency
children.top_down_role: Consistency obligations for duplicated state, projected information, and common decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Component Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility condition ensuring that all component-local solutions agree through their linking relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let component feasible sets be \(F_M\subseteq X_M\) and \(F_S\subseteq X_S\), and let \(L\subseteq X_M\times X_S\) collect all linking relations. A pair of local assignments \((x^M,x^S)\) is cross-component consistent exactly when \(x^M\in F_M\), \(x^S\in F_S\), and \((x^M,x^S)\in L\). For duplicated shared variables indexed by \(K\), this includes \(x_k^M=x_k^S\) for every \(k\in K\). Consequently, the feasible set represented by the coupled architecture is \(F=(F_M\times F_S)\cap L\), rather than the uncoupled Cartesian product alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local component solutions are jointly consistent exactly when each is locally feasible and every linking or shared-variable relation is satisfied.
assumptions_latex: \(F_M\) and \(F_S\) include all component-local domain and constraint restrictions.
\(L\) contains every declared cross-component relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=(F_M\times F_S)\cap L\).

notation.meaning: set satisfying all cross-component linking relations

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a constraint–variable incidence matrix, with \(A_{ji}\neq 0\) exactly when constraint \(j\) depends on variable \(i\). After row and column permutations, a block-angular sparsity pattern has the form \[A=\begin{pmatrix}A_1&0&\cdots&0&B_1\\0&A_2&\cdots&0&B_2\\\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\0&0&\cdots&A_q&B_q\end{pmatrix}.\] Each \(A_r\) contains incidences local to block \(r\), while the columns represented by \(B_r\) are linking variables. Deleting the linking columns disconnects the incidence structure into the \(q\) local blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block-angular incidence matrix consists of independent diagonal blocks joined only through linking-variable columns; removing those columns separates the blocks.

children.title: Decomposition Graphs
children.top_down_role: Graph and hypergraph views of variable, constraint, and block incidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite graph encoding constraint–variable incidence for decomposition analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a model with constraint indices \(J\), variable indices \(I\), and incidence sets \(N(j)\subseteq I\), its decomposition graph is the bipartite graph \(G=(J\mathbin{\dot\cup}I,E)\), where \((j,i)\in E\) if and only if \(i\in N(j)\). A set \(S\subseteq I\) is a variable separator when deleting \(S\) and its incident edges partitions the remaining graph into at least two nonempty connected components. Each component determines a constraint–variable block, while \(S\) determines the linking-variable interface between those blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The decomposition graph is the bipartite constraint–variable incidence graph; variable separators expose blocks and their linking interface.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite.
Incidence means actual dependence of a constraint on a variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=(J\mathbin{\dot\cup}I,E)\) with \((j,i)\in E\iff i\in N(j)\).

notation.meaning: variable separator defining a linking interface

children.title: Graph-Induced Hybrid Partitions
children.top_down_role: Hybrid boundaries suggested by separators, clusters, articulation structure, or repeated subgraphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Induced Hybrid Partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hybrid component partition obtained from connected components after removing a graph separator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(J\mathbin{\dot\cup}I,E)\) be a decomposition graph and let \(S\subseteq I\) be a variable separator. If \(H_1,\ldots,H_q\) are the connected components of \(G-S\), define \(I_r=I\cap V(H_r)\) and \(J_r=J\cap V(H_r)\). Then \((I_1,J_1),\ldots,(I_q,J_q)\) are graph-induced local blocks and \(S\) is their linking-variable set. Assigning each block to an integer-programming or constraint-processing component yields a hybrid partition; all cross-block interaction is mediated by variables in \(S\), because no edge joins distinct components of \(G-S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Removing a variable separator creates incidence-graph components that become local hybrid blocks, with the separator serving as their linking interface.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite bipartite constraint–variable incidence graph.
\(S\subseteq I\) is a separator producing nonempty components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\cap(V(H_r)\times V(H_s))=\varnothing\) for \(r\neq s\), and cross-block interaction is mediated by \(S\).

notation.meaning: connected component of the incidence graph after separator removal
variable and constraint indices in local block r

children.title: Logical–Linear Representation Bridges
children.top_down_role: Representation families that preserve conditional or combinatorial structure across CP and MIP viewpoints.

children.title: Logical-Linear Activation Bridges
children.top_down_role: Logical activation and equivalence interfaces linking discrete semantics to linear constraints.

children.title: Reification Models
children.top_down_role: Representations connecting constraint truth status to explicit logical state.

knowledge_statements.title: Reification Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Boolean representation of the truth value of a constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(x)\) be a constraint predicate on domain \(X\), and let \(b\in\{0,1\}\). A reification model for \(C\) imposes the biconditional \[b=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C(x)\text{ is true}.\] Equivalently, it enforces both \(b=1\Rightarrow C(x)\) and \(b=0\Rightarrow\neg C(x)\). For a linear inequality \(C(x)\equiv a^\top x\le\beta\), an exact mixed-integer encoding must represent both the inequality and its domain-appropriate complement; the required bounds and any strictness convention depend on the domain of \(a^\top x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reification equates a binary variable with a constraint’s truth value, enforcing both the constraint and its complement in opposite binary states.
assumptions_latex: \(C:X\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}\) is a well-defined predicate.
\(b\) is binary.

children.title: Indicator Models
children.top_down_role: Conditional linear or mixed-integer restrictions controlled by discrete activation state.

knowledge_statements.title: Indicator Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way activation of a constraint by a designated binary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C(x)\) be a constraint predicate on domain \(X\), let \(b\in\{0,1\}\), and choose an activation value \(\delta\in\{0,1\}\). An indicator model imposes \[b=\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C(x).\] When \(b\neq\delta\), the indicator relation alone places no restriction corresponding to \(C\) on \(x\). Thus an indicator is generally not a reification: it becomes equivalent to \(b=\delta\Longleftrightarrow C(x)\) only if the reverse implication \(C(x)\Rightarrow b=\delta\), or an equivalent complementary relation, is separately enforced.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indicator activates a constraint at one binary value and imposes no converse implication unless an additional relation supplies it.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a predicate on \(X\).
\(b\) and the activation value \(\delta\) are binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b=\delta\Rightarrow C(x)\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Disjunctive Programming and Its Relation to Integer Programming p. 1

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Disjunctive Programming and Its Relation to Integer Programming p. 1

children.title: Channeling Models
children.top_down_role: Relations maintaining correspondence between alternative variable or constraint viewpoints.

knowledge_statements.title: Channeling Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraints preserving equivalence between two representations of the same decision or logical state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u\in U\) and \(v\in V\) be two representations of the same modeled information, and let \(\phi:U\to V\) be the declared translation. A channeling model adds constraints whose feasible pairs are exactly \[L_\phi=\{(u,v)\in U\times V:v=\phi(u)\}.\] If only selected predicates are shared, channeling instead requires \(P_k(u)\Longleftrightarrow Q_k(v)\) for every declared index \(k\). Exact channeling is sound and complete: every admitted pair represents the same information, and every valid representation pair is admitted. One-way implications provide propagation links but not exact channeling unless their converses follow from other constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Channeling constraints make two component representations equivalent through an exact translation or matching families of logical predicates.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(V\) are declared representation domains.
\(\phi\), or the predicate pairs \((P_k,Q_k)\), specifies the intended semantic correspondence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((u,v)\in L_\phi\iff v=\phi(u)\), or \(P_k(u)\iff Q_k(v)\) for every declared \(k\).

notation.meaning: corresponding predicates on the two representations

children.title: Logical–Linear Bridge Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Semantic preservation and relaxation behavior across logical–linear interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Logical–Linear Bridge Fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact integer-feasible fidelity, distinct from the strength of the formulation's continuous relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^p\times\mathbb{R}^n\) be the feasible set specified by the intended logical semantics, and let \(M\subseteq\{0,1\}^p\times\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^q\) be the integer-feasible set of a logical–linear bridge formulation. The bridge has integer-feasible fidelity when \[\operatorname{proj}_{b,x}(M)=L.\] Equivalently, every point of \(L\) has an auxiliary completion in \(M\), and every point of \(M\) projects into \(L\). If \(\overline M\) denotes the feasible set obtained by relaxing \(b\in\{0,1\}^p\) to \(b\in[0,1]^p\), fidelity alone does not imply \(\operatorname{proj}_{b,x}(\overline M)=\operatorname{conv}(L)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bridge is integer-feasible faithful exactly when projecting its integer-feasible linear model onto the logical and original variables recovers the intended logical feasible set; this alone does not make its continuous relaxation ideal.
assumptions_latex: \(p,n,q\) are nonnegative integers.
\(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^p\times\mathbb{R}^n\) is the feasible set specified by the intended logical semantics.
\(M\subseteq\{0,1\}^p\times\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^q\) is the integer-feasible set of the bridge formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{b,x}(M)=L\).

notation.meaning: integer-feasible bridge set including auxiliary variables
continuous relaxation of the bridge set
projection onto the logical and original variables

children.title: Conditional-Region Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Union-based representations of conditional feasible regions and piecewise structure.

children.title: Disjunctive Models
children.top_down_role: Union-based feasible-region representations and their hybrid solver interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite exclusive disjunction of polyhedral regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\ge 1\) be an integer. For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), let \(m_i\ge 1\), \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{m_i\times n}\), \(d_i\in\mathbb{R}^{m_i}\), and \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_i x\le d_i\}\). An exclusive disjunctive model represents \[x\in\bigcup_{i=1}^k P_i.\] Its selector form uses \(z\in\{0,1\}^k\) and imposes \[\sum_{i=1}^k z_i=1,\qquad z_i=1\Rightarrow A_i x\le d_i\quad\text{for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.\] This selector system projects onto exactly \(\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\). A linear or extended encoding is an exact formulation of the disjunction when its projection onto \(x\) is this union.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exclusive disjunctive model places a decision vector in one of finitely many polyhedral regions; an exact selector encoding projects to precisely their union.
assumptions_latex: \(k,n\) and \(m_1,\ldots,m_k\) are positive integers.
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(A_i\in\mathbb{R}^{m_i\times n}\), \(d_i\in\mathbb{R}^{m_i}\), and \(P_i=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A_i x\le d_i\}\).
Exactly one alternative is selected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\bigcup_{i=1}^kP_i\) if and only if there exists \(z\in\{0,1\}^k\) such that \(\sum_{i=1}^kz_i=1\) and \(z_i=1\Rightarrow x\in P_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\).

children.title: Trigger Models
children.top_down_role: Event-like or condition-controlled activation of constraints and substructures.

knowledge_statements.title: Trigger Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-way activation; the converse requires an additional implication.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n,m\) be positive integers, \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(P=\{x\in X:Ax\le d\}\). For \(b\in\{0,1\}\), a trigger model imposes \[b=1\Rightarrow x\in P.\] Its semantic feasible set is \[T=\{(b,x)\in\{0,1\}\times X:b=0\text{ or }Ax\le d\}.\] Thus \(b=0\) leaves only \(x\in X\). Equivalence between activation and membership requires the additional implication \(x\in P\Rightarrow b=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trigger model activates a specified region when a binary variable equals one; trigger inactivity imposes only the ambient restrictions.
assumptions_latex: \(n,m\) are positive integers.
\(b\in\{0,1\}\) is a trigger variable.
\(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^m\).
\(P=\{x\in X:Ax\le d\}\) is the region activated by the trigger.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is \(\{(b,x)\in\{0,1\}\times X:b=0\text{ or }x\in P\}\).

notation.meaning: ambient domain of the controlled variables
semantic feasible set of the trigger model

source_refs.locator: Chapter 3. Building linear programming models p. 21

children.title: Piecewise Models
children.top_down_role: Segmented relations, costs, and feasible regions represented for hybrid inference.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph representation of a finite single-valued piecewise-affine function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k,n\) be positive integers, let \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and set \(D=\bigcup_{i=1}^kD_i\). For each \(i\), let \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(c_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(f_i(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\) on \(D_i\). Assume \[f_i(x)=f_j(x)\quad\text{for all }i,j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\text{ and all }x\in D_i\cap D_j.\] Then \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\), defined by \(f(x)=f_i(x)\) whenever \(x\in D_i\), is well defined, and its graph is \[\operatorname{graph}(f)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:x\in D_i,\ y=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite piecewise-affine function is represented by the union of its region-specific affine graphs, provided the affine expressions agree wherever their regions overlap.
assumptions_latex: \(k,n\) are positive integers and \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(a_i\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(c_i\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(f_i(x)=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\) on \(D_i\).
\(f_i(x)=f_j(x)\) for every \(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\) and every \(x\in D_i\cap D_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(D=\bigcup_{i=1}^kD_i\), the induced function \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfies \(\operatorname{graph}(f)=\bigcup_{i=1}^k\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:x\in D_i,\ y=a_i^{\mathsf T}x+c_i\}\).

children.title: Conditional-Region Overlap
children.top_down_role: Interactions among alternative regions, activation conditions, and shared boundary states.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional-Region Overlap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantic compatibility conditions for overlapping alternative descriptions or simultaneous conditional constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k\) be a positive integer, let \(D_i\subseteq X\) be the activation region of branch \(i\), and let \(R_i\subseteq X\times Y\) be its relation. For \(x\in X\), define \[I(x)=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}:x\in D_i\},\qquad Y_i(x)=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in R_i\}.\] If the active branches are alternative descriptions of the same relation, overlap is consistent when \[Y_i(x)=Y_j(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in X\text{ and all }i,j\in I(x).\] If all active branches are imposed simultaneously, feasibility at \(x\) instead requires \[\bigcap_{i\in I(x)}Y_i(x)\ne\varnothing\] whenever \(I(x)\ne\varnothing\). Pairwise nonempty intersections alone are not sufficient for simultaneous feasibility when more than two branches are active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overlapping alternative descriptions must admit identical outputs, whereas simultaneously active branches must have a common output across the entire active set.
assumptions_latex: \(k\) is a positive integer and \(X,Y\) are sets.
For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,k\}\), \(D_i\subseteq X\) is an activation region and \(R_i\subseteq X\times Y\) is the branch relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Alternative-description consistency requires \(Y_i(x)=Y_j(x)\) for all \(i,j\in I(x)\); simultaneous-branch feasibility requires \(\bigcap_{i\in I(x)}Y_i(x)\ne\varnothing\) whenever \(I(x)\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: outputs admitted by branch i at x
indices of branches active at x

children.title: Multi-View Extended Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-state and projected representations that expose different inference structures.

children.title: Extended Models
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-state formulations that expose additional structure to hybrid solvers.

assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is the set to be represented.
\(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+q}\) is described using original variables \(x\) and auxiliary variables \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is an extended model of \(S\) when \(S=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extended formulation under coordinate projection.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Disjunctive Programming and Extended Formulations p. 69

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A set \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+q}\), expressed in original variables \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and auxiliary variables \(y\in\mathbb{R}^q\), is an extended model of \(S\) when \[S=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^q,\ (x,y)\in Q\}.\] If \(Q\) is a polyhedron, it is an extended linear formulation; integrality restrictions must be included in \(Q\) before taking the stated projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended model introduces auxiliary variables while preserving the original feasible set exactly after projection.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended Models

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Disjunctive Programming and Extended Formulations p. 69

children.title: Projected Models
children.top_down_role: Representations expressed over reduced or coordinating variable spaces.

assumptions_latex: \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+q}\) is a feasible set in variables \((x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projected model is \(P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x:\exists y,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential elimination of auxiliary coordinates.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Disjunctive Programming and Extended Formulations p. 69

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+q}\), the model obtained by retaining \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and eliminating \(y\in\mathbb{R}^q\) is \[P=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^q,\ (x,y)\in Q\}.\] Hence a constraint in the projected model is valid precisely when it holds for every \(x\) having an auxiliary completion in \(Q\). When \(Q\) is polyhedral, \(P\) is polyhedral, although an explicit inequality description may be much larger.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projected model removes auxiliary coordinates existentially and retains exactly those original-variable points having a feasible completion.
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Models

children.title: Multiple-Viewpoint Models
children.top_down_role: Parallel representations of common decisions for distinct inference mechanisms.

assumptions_latex: A semantic object has feasible realization set \(S\).
For each viewpoint \(r\), \(E_r\) maps its variable space \(X_r\) to semantic realizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The joint model is \(M=\{(x^1,\ldots,x^m):E_1(x^1)=\cdots=E_m(x^m)\in S\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parallel encodings of one semantic decision object.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Structured linear programming models p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be the feasible semantic realizations of one decision object. For viewpoints \(r=1,\ldots,m\), let \(x^r\in X_r\) and let \(E_r:X_r\to U\) decode viewpoint \(r\). A multiple-viewpoint model is the joint representation \[M=\{(x^1,\ldots,x^m):E_1(x^1)=\cdots=E_m(x^m)\in S\}.\] Each viewpoint may use different variables or constraints, but every feasible tuple must decode to the same semantic realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-viewpoint model uses several encodings of one object and constrains every feasible encoding tuple to denote the same feasible realization.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Viewpoint Models

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Structured linear programming models p. 45

A source on multiple viewpoints or redundant modeling with explicit channeling semantics is required.

children.title: Viewpoint Consistency Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Information exchange and semantic consistency across extended, projected, or duplicated viewpoints.

assumptions_latex: Viewpoints \(r\) and \(s\) have domains \(X_r,X_s\) and decoding maps \(E_r,E_s\).
\(C_{rs}\subseteq X_r\times X_s\) is their interface relation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface is exact when \((u,v)\in C_{rs}\) if and only if \(E_r(u)=E_s(v)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise exact channeling between semantic encodings.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. Structured linear programming models p. 45

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For encodings \(u\in X_r\) and \(v\in X_s\) with decoding maps \(E_r\) and \(E_s\), an exact viewpoint-consistency interface is a relation \(C_{rs}\subseteq X_r\times X_s\) satisfying \[(u,v)\in C_{rs}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E_r(u)=E_s(v).\] The forward implication prevents inconsistent joint assignments; the reverse implication ensures that the interface does not discard semantically identical pairs. A one-way channeling interface satisfies only the forward implication and is therefore generally incomplete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact consistency interface accepts precisely those pairs of viewpoint assignments that decode to the same semantic object.
knowledge_statements.title: Viewpoint Consistency Interfaces

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 4. Structured linear programming models p. 45

A direct source on channeling or multiple-viewpoint consistency is required.

children.title: Global-Constraint Relaxation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Mathematical relaxations and decompositions attached to global or structured CP constraints.

children.title: Polyhedral Global-Constraint Relaxation Pair
children.top_down_role: Polyhedral and auxiliary-variable views of structured constraint feasible sets.

children.title: Linear Global-Constraint Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Direct polyhedral approximations of global-constraint feasible sets.

assumptions_latex: \(G\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) is the feasible set of a global constraint within its bounded variable domain.
\(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) is a polyhedron in the original variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\) is a valid linear relaxation when \(G\subseteq P\); it is ideal when \(P=\operatorname{conv}(G)\).

notation.meaning: integer tuples satisfying the global constraint

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct relaxation in the global constraint's original variables.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Fundamental concepts and results on polyhedra, linear inequalities, and linear programming p. 85

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) contain exactly the bounded-domain tuples satisfying a global constraint. A direct linear global-constraint relaxation is a polyhedron \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\] in the original variables such that \(G\subseteq P\). It is exact at integer points when \(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=G\), and ideal when \(P=\operatorname{conv}(G)\). For minimization, replacing \(G\) by \(P\) yields a valid lower bound for every linear objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct linear relaxation contains all tuples satisfying a global constraint; ideality means it equals their convex hull.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear Global-Constraint Relaxations

children.title: Extended Global-Constraint Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary-variable relaxations exposing stronger or more structured feasible-set descriptions.

assumptions_latex: \(G\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) is the feasible set of a bounded-domain global constraint.
\(Q=\{(x,y):Bx+Cy\le d\}\) is a polyhedron with auxiliary variables \(y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is an extended relaxation when \(G\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\), and it is ideal when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(G)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary-variable polyhedral relaxation of a global constraint.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Disjunctive Programming and Extended Formulations p. 69

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^n\) be the feasible tuples of a bounded-domain global constraint. An extended linear relaxation is a polyhedron \[Q=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+q}:Bx+Cy\le d\}\] satisfying \[G\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(Q).\] It is exact at integer points when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\cap\mathbb{Z}^n=G\), and ideal when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)=\operatorname{conv}(G)\). Auxiliary variables may provide a compact description unavailable in the original space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended global-constraint relaxation uses auxiliary variables and is valid when its original-variable projection contains every feasible tuple.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended Global-Constraint Relaxations

children.title: Direct–Extended Relaxation Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Size, strength, projection behavior, and inference cost across the two relaxation forms.

assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a direct relaxation of the same feasible set represented by an extended relaxation \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+q}\).
Formulation size counts variables plus explicitly stated linear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\) is at least as strong as \(P\) exactly when \(\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\subseteq P\), while its size and optimization cost must be assessed in the extended space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strength-versus-size comparison for direct and extended polyhedral relaxations.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a direct relaxation and \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+q}\) an extended relaxation of the same feasible set. Writing \(R=\operatorname{proj}_x(Q)\), the extension is at least as strong precisely when \(R\subseteq P\), and strictly stronger when \(R\subsetneq P\). Strength alone does not determine computational preference: \(Q\) can use fewer inequalities than an explicit description of \(R\), but introduces variables and changes linear-algebra, propagation, and separation costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended relaxation is stronger when its projection is smaller, but compactness and computational cost depend on inequalities, auxiliaries, and solver operations.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct–Extended Relaxation Tradeoffs

children.title: Network-Combinatorial Relaxation Family
children.top_down_role: Flow, matching, assignment, and combinatorial bounds associated with global constraints.

children.title: Network Global-Constraint Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Flow, path, matching, and assignment network views of structured constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Global-Constraint Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flow-based extended relaxation of a finite-domain global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be the assignments satisfying a global constraint, let \(G=(V,E)\) be a directed graph with node–arc incidence matrix \(A\), and let \[Q=\{f\in\mathbb R^{|E|}:Af=b,\;\ell\leq f\leq u\}.\] Given a linear map \(\pi:\mathbb R^{|E|}\to\mathbb R^n\), the pair \((Q,\pi)\) defines a valid network relaxation of \(S\) when \(S\subseteq\pi(Q)\). If the formulation is constructed from integral flows, one may additionally require \(S\subseteq\pi(Q\cap\mathbb Z^{|E|})\), which implies the continuous validity condition. The continuous relaxation is \(R_N=\pi(Q)\), and it is exact when \(R_N=\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network relaxation projects a capacitated flow polyhedron to a region containing all feasible assignments. Its continuous relaxation is exact precisely when that projection equals the convex hull of the feasible assignments.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite.
\(A\) is the node–arc incidence matrix of \(G\).
\(\pi\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq R_N=\pi(Q)\)

notation.meaning: feasible integer assignments of the global constraint
linear map from flow variables to assignment variables

review_flags: network-specific formulation support should be checked

children.title: Combinatorial Global-Constraint Relaxations
children.top_down_role: Non-network combinatorial bounds and relaxations derived from discrete structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Global-Constraint Relaxations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation obtained from a tractable combinatorial superset or inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be the feasible assignments of a global constraint. A combinatorial relaxation is a tractable set \(T\supseteq S\), described by a combinatorial structure or a polynomial-time membership, optimization, or separation procedure. Its convex relaxation is a polyhedron or convex set \(R_C\) satisfying \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq R_C\subseteq\operatorname{conv}(T)\). Valid inequalities separated over \(R_C\) may be added to the integer-programming model without excluding any point of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combinatorial relaxation replaces the global constraint by a tractable superset or valid-inequality system whose convex region contains every feasible assignment.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite.
Optimization, membership, or separation over the chosen relaxation is computationally available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq R_C\)

children.title: Network Representability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes where network formulations capture, approximate, or fail to capture relevant combinatorics.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Representability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity and exactness boundaries for a prescribed network formulation class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a class \(\mathcal N_k\) of network formulations having encoding size at most \(k\). A feasible-assignment set \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) is exactly network-representable in this class if some \((Q,\pi)\in\mathcal N_k\) satisfies \(S=\pi(Q\cap\mathbb Z^{|E|})\) and \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\pi(Q)\). If only \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subsetneq\pi(Q)\) holds, the formulation is merely a relaxation. If \(S\nsubseteq\pi(Q\cap\mathbb Z^{|E|})\), it is invalid. Thus representability is always relative to the permitted graph, side constraints, projection, and size bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network model is exact only when both its integral-flow projection and continuous projection match the constraint; strict containment gives a relaxation, while missing feasible assignments makes it invalid.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is finite.
The allowed formulation class \(\mathcal N_k\) and its size measure are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(S)=\pi(Q)\), or \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subsetneq\pi(Q)\), or \(S\nsubseteq\pi(Q\cap\mathbb Z^{|E|})\)

notation.meaning: admissible network formulations of size at most k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational exactness boundary for extended relaxations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the cited general section on linear-programming relaxations does not specifically support the network formulation class, encoding-size restriction, or two-part exact-representability criterion. A dedicated network or extended-formulation source is required.

children.title: Multi-View Global-Constraint Representation
children.top_down_role: Multiple representations retained to combine propagation and relaxation strength.

children.title: Decomposed Global-Constraint Views
children.top_down_role: Smaller component constraints used to expose local inference or relaxation structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposed Global-Constraint Views
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primitive-constraint view equivalent to a global constraint after auxiliary-variable projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq X\) be the relation defined by a global constraint. A decomposed view introduces auxiliary variables \(y\in Y\) and primitive relations \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) such that \[S=\{x\in X:\exists y\in Y,\;(x,y)\in\bigcap_{j=1}^m C_j\}.\] The decomposition is logically exact by this projection equality. Its propagation need not equal propagation by a dedicated global propagator, because enforcing a chosen local consistency on each \(C_j\) may leave values that global consistency on \(S\) would remove.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposed view replaces one global relation with primitive constraints and auxiliaries whose projection is exact, although local propagation over the decomposition can be weaker.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite Cartesian products of variable domains.
Each primitive relation \(C_j\) has an available propagator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=\operatorname{proj}_X\!\left(\bigcap_{j=1}^m C_j\right)\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and projection equality are mathematically coherent, but the cited general CP section does not inspectably support the decomposition-specific claim that primitive propagation may be weaker than a dedicated global propagator.

children.title: Redundant Global-Constraint Views
children.top_down_role: Additional equivalent or implied representations retained for complementary inference.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Global-Constraint Views
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous equivalent representations retained to strengthen inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq X\) be a global-constraint relation. Views \(V_1,\ldots,V_r\) are redundant exact views when, for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,r\}\), view \(V_i\) uses variables \((x,y_i)\) and satisfies \[S=\{x\in X:\exists y_i,\;(x,y_i)\in V_i\}.\] Posting all views preserves the feasible assignments because \[\bigcap_{i=1}^r\operatorname{proj}_X(V_i)=S.\] The views may nevertheless induce different relaxations or propagation operators. Synchronization constraints are required whenever corresponding quantities are represented by distinct variables across views.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundant exact views are individually equivalent representations posted together. They preserve the original feasible assignments but may expose different relaxations or propagation deductions.
assumptions_latex: All views represent the same original-variable vector \(x\).
Auxiliary variables belonging to different views are existentially quantified.
Distinct variables representing the same original quantity are synchronized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcap_{i=1}^r\operatorname{proj}_X(V_i)=S\)

notation.meaning: auxiliary variables local to the i-th view

children.title: Multi-View Inference Complementarity
children.top_down_role: Propagation and relaxation gains obtained from retaining interacting constraint views.

knowledge_statements.title: Multi-View Inference Complementarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly stronger closure obtained by alternating incomparable sound view propagators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_1,\ldots,P_r\) be monotone, contracting, sound propagators on finite domain states, with \(P_i(D)\subseteq D\). Starting from \(D^0=D\), apply the propagators fairly until a common fixed point \(D^*\) is reached. The views are inference-complementary at \(D\) when \(D^*\subsetneq P_i(D)\) for at least two indices \(i\), so deductions communicated from one view enable additional deductions in another. Finiteness and contraction imply termination, while soundness ensures that no feasible assignment contained in \(D\) is removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Views are inference-complementary when fair propagation to their common fixed point removes strictly more values than at least two views do separately, without removing feasible assignments.
assumptions_latex: The domain-state lattice is finite.
Every \(P_i\) is monotone, contracting, and solution-preserving.
The propagation schedule is fair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D^*\subseteq P_i(D)\subseteq D\), with \(D^*\subsetneq P_i(D)\) for at least two \(i\)

notation.meaning: sound propagator induced by view i

review_flags: fixed-point formulation requires dedicated propagation source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role is appropriate and the fixed-point formulation is plausible, but the cited modeling section does not specifically support fair chaotic iteration, termination, common-fixed-point semantics, or the proposed two-view strictness criterion.

children.title: Redundancy Overhead Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Memory, synchronization, and inference-cost regimes limiting redundant representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Redundancy Overhead Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost boundary beyond which an additional exact view has no modeled benefit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a baseline search using \(N_0\) processed nodes at cost \(c_0\) per node, suppose a redundant view changes these quantities to \(N_1\) and \(c_0+c_v+c_s\), where \(c_v\) is its inference cost and \(c_s\) its synchronization cost. Under the additive node-cost model, the view is beneficial exactly when \[N_1(c_0+c_v+c_s)<N_0c_0.\] Equality is the overhead boundary; the view is detrimental when the inequality reverses. Logical redundancy alone provides no guarantee that the reduction in \(N_1\) offsets representation, propagation, and synchronization costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A redundant view pays off only when its search reduction exceeds its per-node inference and synchronization overhead; equality defines the modeled break-even boundary.
assumptions_latex: Search effort is measured by processed nodes.
Per-node costs are represented by nonnegative constants.
Construction costs are absent or amortized into \(c_v+c_s\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_1(c_0+c_v+c_s)\lesseqgtr N_0c_0\) determines benefit, break-even, or loss

notation.meaning: additional inference and synchronization cost per node

review_flags: dedicated empirical or complexity source needed
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The break-even inequality is correct under the stated additive cost model and fits a failure-boundary leaf, but no source supports this particular overhead model or its applicability to redundant global-constraint views.

children.title: Hybrid Formulation Quality
children.top_down_role: Comparative quality of representations as seen by both propagation and relaxation engines.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Conforti, Cornuéjols, and Zambelli, Sections 2.2, 4.9, and 4.10

children.title: Relaxation-Propagation Strength Coupling
children.top_down_role: Joint comparison of bound quality, domain reduction, and infeasibility detection.

children.title: Relaxation Strength
children.top_down_role: Bound quality, feasible-region approximation, and relaxation-based infeasibility detection.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-inclusion ordering of valid continuous relaxations for one minimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb Z^n\) be the feasible set and let \(R_1,R_2\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) satisfy \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\subseteq R_i\). Relaxation \(R_1\) is at least as strong as \(R_2\) when \(R_1\subseteq R_2\), and strictly stronger when the inclusion is strict. For any objective vector \(c\) in a minimization problem, this ordering implies \[\inf_{x\in R_2}c^\top x\leq\inf_{x\in R_1}c^\top x\leq\inf_{x\in S}c^\top x.\] Thus the stronger relaxation gives a bound no worse for every linear objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation is stronger when its feasible region is contained in another valid relaxation; for minimization, its optimal value is consequently a no-weaker lower bound.
assumptions_latex: Both relaxations contain \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\).
The displayed infima are well-defined in the extended real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\subseteq R_2\Longrightarrow \inf_{R_2}c^\top x\leq\inf_{R_1}c^\top x\leq\inf_S c^\top x\)

children.title: Propagation Strength
children.top_down_role: Domain reduction and infeasibility detection produced by constraint inference.

knowledge_statements.title: Propagation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise ordering of sound domain-reduction operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal D\) be a finite lattice of domain states ordered by componentwise inclusion, and let \(P_1,P_2:\mathcal D\to\mathcal D\) be sound contracting propagators for the same constraint. Propagator \(P_1\) is at least as strong as \(P_2\) when \(P_1(D)\subseteq P_2(D)\) for every \(D\in\mathcal D\). It is strictly stronger when this inclusion is strict for at least one state. This comparison concerns values removed at propagation closure and is independent of the runtime required to compute that closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One propagator is stronger when, on every domain state, it retains no more values than another sound propagator, with strictness witnessed by some state.
assumptions_latex: Both propagators preserve every feasible assignment.
Both propagators are contracting on the same finite domain-state lattice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_1\succeq P_2\iff (\forall D\in\mathcal D)\;P_1(D)\subseteq P_2(D)\)
review_flags: propagator-order definition requires dedicated CP source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pointwise operator ordering is a coherent definition for this leaf, but the cited general CP section does not inspectably support the precise propagator-strength order. The phrase concerning propagation closure also requires a source clarifying whether each \(P_i\) is an idempotent closure or a single propagation operator.

children.title: Strength Complementarity
children.top_down_role: Regimes where relaxation bounds and propagation reductions reinforce or duplicate one another.

knowledge_statements.title: Strength Complementarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined benefit from relaxation bounds and domain propagation without a dominance requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(D)\) be a valid continuous relaxation under domain state \(D\), and let \(P(D)\subseteq D\) be a sound propagation closure. Their coupled closure alternates domain filtering and relaxation rebuilding until \((D^*,R^*)\) is stable. Relaxation and propagation are strength-complementary at \(D\) when propagation strictly tightens the relaxation, \(R(P(D))\subsetneq R(D)\), and relaxation-derived deductions subsequently tighten the propagated domains, \(D^*\subsetneq P(D)\). Neither mechanism must dominate the other pointwise; complementarity is witnessed by strict improvement in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation and propagation are complementary when propagation strictly tightens the relaxation and relaxation-based deductions then strictly reduce the propagated domains.
assumptions_latex: All relaxations remain valid for the current domains.
All domain deductions are solution-preserving.
The alternating closure terminates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(P(D))\subsetneq R(D)\) and \(D^*\subsetneq P(D)\)

notation.meaning: relaxation restricted by domain state D

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits, but the relaxation-derived domain-deduction operator is not defined, so the alternating closure and the condition \(D^*\subsetneq P(D)\) cannot be checked formally. No source supports the proposed bidirectional complementarity criterion.

children.title: Strength Mismatch Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where strong performance in one inference channel does not transfer to the other.

knowledge_statements.title: Strength Mismatch Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regimes where relaxation and propagation orders disagree.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two hybrid formulations \(H_1=(R_1,P_1)\) and \(H_2=(R_2,P_2)\) for the same feasible set. A strength mismatch occurs when their relaxation and propagation orders conflict: either \(R_1\subsetneq R_2\) while some domain state \(D\) satisfies \(P_2(D)\subsetneq P_1(D)\), or the symmetric condition holds. An extreme mismatch occurs when one formulation has an exact relaxation but weak propagation, or domain-complete propagation but a strict relaxation. Consequently, relaxation dominance alone does not imply propagation dominance, nor does propagation dominance imply relaxation dominance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mismatch occurs when one formulation has the tighter relaxation but another performs stronger domain filtering; neither strength order generally determines the other.
assumptions_latex: Both formulations represent the same feasible assignments.
Each \(R_i\) is valid and each \(P_i\) is sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_1\subsetneq R_2\) and \((\exists D)\;P_2(D)\subsetneq P_1(D)\), or symmetrically
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: mismatch defined by conflicting partial orders
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conflicting-order condition is mathematically plausible and fits a failure-boundary leaf, but no source supports it as a recognized hybrid-formulation regime. The additional terms “weak propagation” and “domain-complete propagation” are not formally defined.

children.title: Representation-Inference Cost Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs among auxiliary state, relaxation size, propagation expense, and update cost.

children.title: Representation Size
children.top_down_role: Variable, constraint, auxiliary-state, and relaxation footprint of hybrid representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Size
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit structural and bit-encoding size measures for a hybrid formulation family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a hybrid formulation \(F\), let \(n_o(F)\) be the number of original variables, \(n_a(F)\) the number of auxiliary variables, \(n_c(F)\) the number of posted constraints, and \(n_z(F)\) the number of explicitly stored coefficient entries or incidences. Define its structural size by \[s(F)=n_o(F)+n_a(F)+n_c(F)+n_z(F).\] Its encoding size \(L(F)\) is the total number of bits needed to encode its symbols, indices, domains, coefficients, bounds, and nonfixed propagator descriptions. For an instance family \(\mathcal I\) with a formulation \(F(I)\) for each \(I\in\mathcal I\), the representation family is polynomial-size when there exists a polynomial \(p\) such that \[L(F(I))\leq p(L(I))\qquad\text{for every }I\in\mathcal I.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Structural representation size counts original variables, auxiliary variables, posted constraints, and stored coefficients or incidences without overlap. Bit size counts their encodings. A formulation family is polynomial-size when one polynomial bounds its encoding length in terms of instance encoding length.
assumptions_latex: All numeric data have finite binary encodings.
Fixed library propagators have constant-size identifiers; otherwise their descriptions are included in \(L(F)\).
Each instance \(I\in\mathcal I\) is assigned a formulation \(F(I)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s(F)=n_o(F)+n_a(F)+n_c(F)+n_z(F)\), and polynomial size requires \((\exists p)(\forall I\in\mathcal I)\;L(F(I))\leq p(L(I))\)

notation.meaning: bit-encoding length of input instance I

review_flags: structural size formula is an explicit local convention

children.title: Inference Cost
children.top_down_role: Computational expense of propagation, relaxation, synchronization, and incremental updates.

assumptions_latex: The hybrid formulation and its inference routines are fixed.
The resource measure assigns a nonnegative cost to every admissible solver state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Lower values of \(I_{\mathcal A}(\mathcal S)\) mean that the representation supports cheaper inference under algorithm \(\mathcal A\) and resource \(R\).

notation.meaning: family of admissible solver states for the formulation
resource consumed by one inference call

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case computational cost of one representation-dependent inference operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a formulation with admissible solver-state family \(\mathcal S\), inference algorithm \(\mathcal A\), and resource measure \(R\), its inference cost is \[I_{\mathcal A}(\mathcal S)=\sup_{s\in\mathcal S}R(\mathcal A,s).\] The resource may count arithmetic operations, oracle calls, memory, or elapsed time, but must be fixed before formulations are compared. An average-case variant replaces the supremum by \(\mathbb E_{s\sim\mu}[R(\mathcal A,s)]\) for an explicitly specified distribution \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inference cost is the fixed worst-case or explicitly distributed average resource consumption of an inference routine over admissible solver states.
knowledge_statements.title: Inference Cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited constraint-programming overview does not substantiate this particular worst-case/average resource functional. The domain and codomain of R and the distinction between formulation cost and algorithm-state cost also require an authoritative complexity or inference-cost source.

children.title: Size–Inference Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Structural choices exchanging larger representations for stronger or cheaper repeated inference.

assumptions_latex: Two formulations encode the same feasible decisions and objective values.
Representation size and inference cost are measured under fixed conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither formulation dominates the other exactly when one has smaller size and the other has smaller inference cost.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto comparison of semantically equivalent hybrid formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For semantically equivalent formulations \(F_1\) and \(F_2\), define \[F_1\preceq F_2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S(F_1)\le S(F_2)\ \text{ and }\ I(F_1)\le I(F_2).\] A strict improvement requires at least one strict inequality. The size-inference tradeoff is the set of nondominated formulations: increasing representation size is justified only when the resulting reduction in inference cost is relevant to the chosen resource model, and decreasing size is justified only when the induced inference cost remains acceptable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent formulations are compared by Pareto dominance in representation size and inference cost; tradeoffs occur when neither formulation improves both measures.
knowledge_statements.title: Size–Inference Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto relation is coherent and fits the leaf, but the cited modeling chapters do not specifically support the proposed size–inference measures or the normative justification claims.

children.title: Semantic-Numerical Fidelity Interface
children.top_down_role: Translation loss, coefficient quality, and tension between logical and floating-point semantics.

children.title: Semantic Fidelity
children.top_down_role: Preservation of logical meaning across CP, MIP, and translated representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Semantic Fidelity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasible-set and objective preservation under hybrid translation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) be the original decision domain, let \(F\subseteq D\) be the original feasible set, let \(E\) be the encoded feasible set, and let \(\pi:E\to D\) be the declared projection. The encoding is semantically faithful when \[\pi(E)=F.\] Thus every encoded feasible point projects to an original feasible decision, and every original feasible decision has at least one encoded extension. If \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) and \(\tilde f:E\to\mathbb R\) are the original and encoded objective functions, respectively, objective fidelity additionally requires \[\forall y\in E,\qquad \tilde f(y)=f(\pi(y)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hybrid encoding is semantically faithful when projection preserves exactly all feasible decisions and, when objectives are present, preserves their objective values pointwise.
assumptions_latex: The original model has a decision domain \(D\) and feasible set \(F\subseteq D\).
The hybrid encoding has a feasible set \(E\) and a declared projection \(\pi:E\to D\).
When objective fidelity is considered, the objective maps are \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) and \(\tilde f:E\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The encoding is semantically faithful exactly when \(\pi(E)=F\), with objective fidelity additionally requiring \(\tilde f=f\circ\pi\) on \(E\).

notation.meaning: encoded feasible set, including auxiliary variables
projection from encoded points to original decisions

children.title: Numerical Quality
children.top_down_role: Coefficient scaling, tolerance sensitivity, conditioning, and floating-point robustness.

assumptions_latex: The numerical formulation is represented by finite-precision coefficients and residual functions.
All reported quality measures use a fixed scaling convention and arithmetic precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Smaller coefficient range and condition estimates, together with larger normalized feasibility margins, indicate better numerical quality under the fixed convention.

notation.meaning: ratio of largest to smallest nonzero scaled coefficient magnitude
condition estimate for the relevant linearized system

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A convention-dependent quality vector for finite-precision hybrid formulations.

source_refs.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under a fixed row and variable scaling, define the numerical-quality descriptor of a formulation as \(Q=(\rho,\kappa,m)\), where \(\rho\) is the ratio between the largest and smallest nonzero scaled coefficient magnitudes, \(\kappa\) is a stated condition estimate for each linear system used by inference, and \(m\) is the smallest normalized distance of certified decisions from a feasibility boundary. Numerical quality improves as \(\rho\) and \(\kappa\) decrease and \(m\) increases; comparisons without a common scaling and precision convention are undefined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numerical quality records coefficient range, conditioning, and normalized feasibility margins under a fixed scaling and precision convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Quality

source_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation and Decomposition Methods for Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited numerical-results section does not support the proposed descriptor Q. A single κ is also inconsistent with referring to condition estimates for multiple inference systems, and the margin m is not universally defined for a formulation.

children.title: Logical–Numerical Consistency
children.top_down_role: Agreement between discrete semantics and tolerance-based numerical decisions.

assumptions_latex: An exact semantic predicate \(P:D\to\{0,1\}\) is fixed.
The numerical encoding has an acceptance predicate \(P_{\tau}:D\to\{0,1\}\) under declared tolerances \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Logical-numerical consistency holds precisely when \(P_{\tau}(x)=P(x)\) for every admissible decision \(x\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Agreement between exact logical semantics and tolerance-based numerical acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P(x)\) be the exact logical feasibility predicate on \(D\), and let \(P_{\tau}(x)\) be the predicate implemented by the numerical encoding and its declared tolerances \(\tau\). The interface is logically-numerically consistent on \(D\) exactly when \[\forall x\in D,\qquad P_{\tau}(x)=P(x).\] One-sided consistency may instead be declared explicitly: sound acceptance requires \(P_{\tau}(x)=1\Rightarrow P(x)=1\), while complete acceptance requires \(P(x)=1\Rightarrow P_{\tau}(x)=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Logical-numerical consistency means numerical acceptance agrees with exact logical feasibility, or satisfies an explicitly declared one-sided implication.
knowledge_statements.title: Logical–Numerical Consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact and one-sided consistency conditions are coherent, but the cited CP overview does not substantiate the finite-precision acceptance predicate or its tolerance semantics.

children.title: Translation Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes where reformulation, approximation, or numerical tolerance changes intended model behavior.

assumptions_latex: The implication \(z=0\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) is encoded by \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b+Mz\).
The binary variable satisfies \(z\in\{0,1\}\), and feasibility is tested in finite precision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Too small an \(M\) destroys semantic fidelity; excessively large \(M\) enlarges tolerance-scaled acceptance errors and weakens the relaxation.

notation.meaning: maximum required relaxation over the bounded domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Big-M translation exhibits both semantic and finite-precision failure thresholds.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Disjunctive Programming and Its Relation to Integer Programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the implication \(z=0\Rightarrow a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\), let \(M^{\star}=\sup_{x\in D}(a^{\mathsf T}x-b)\) over the bounded admissible domain \(D\). The encoding \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b+Mz\) is semantically invalid when \(M<M^{\star}\), because it excludes admissible points with \(z=1\). Conversely, under a relative row tolerance \(\varepsilon\), acceptance can permit residuals proportional to \(\varepsilon\max\{1,|b|,|M|\}\); hence unnecessarily large \(M\) creates a numerical-consistency boundary and weakens continuous inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A big-M translation fails semantically below the required bound and becomes numerically unreliable or inferentially weak when the bound is excessive.
knowledge_statements.title: Translation Failure Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Disjunctive Programming and Its Relation to Integer Programming p. 1

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The semantic lower-bound phenomenon is standard, but the claimed tolerance scaling is solver-specific and unsupported by the cited sources. The convention for nonnegative M and the precise continuous-relaxation claim also need a directly relevant source.

children.title: Single-Tree Constraint Integer Programming
children.top_down_role: Integrated architectures in which general constraints, mathematical relaxations, propagation, learning, and branching share one search tree.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: CIP paradigm and main design concepts

children.title: CIP Constraint-Handler Abstraction
children.top_down_role: Unified modeling and constraint-class ownership of semantics, inference, relaxation, and enforcement.

children.title: Constraint Feasibility Semantics Interface
children.top_down_role: Handler responsibility for recognizing satisfaction of a constraint class.

children.title: Constraint Semantics
children.top_down_role: Constraint-class meaning and the states recognized by a handler.

assumptions_latex: A constraint instance \(c\) has an admissible assignment domain \(D_c\).
Its handler exposes a total truth predicate on complete assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An assignment satisfies \(c\) exactly when it belongs to \(F_c=\{x\in D_c:S_c(x)=1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extensional semantics of a constraint-handler instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The semantics of a constraint instance \(c\) with admissible assignment domain \(D_c\) is a predicate \[S_c:D_c\to\{0,1\}.\] Its feasible set is \(F_c=\{x\in D_c:S_c(x)=1\}\). Auxiliary data, propagation state, relaxations, and enforcement procedures do not change this set unless they are explicitly part of \(D_c\) and \(S_c\). Two handler representations of \(c\) are semantically equivalent when they define the same feasible set after projection onto the declared decision variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint semantics is the exact predicate, and hence feasible set, assigned to a constraint instance over its declared domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Semantics

children.title: Feasibility Checking
children.top_down_role: Handler evaluation of integral, fractional, partial, or relaxation candidates.

assumptions_latex: Each constraint \(c\) has a nonnegative violation function \(v_c\) with \(v_c(x)=0\) exactly for semantic feasibility.
The evaluator returns a certified interval \([\ell_c(x),u_c(x)]\) containing \(v_c(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The checker returns feasible, infeasible, or unknown without making an unsupported decision when the certified interval straddles the tolerance boundary.

notation.meaning: exact nonnegative violation of constraint c
certified lower and upper violation bounds

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-valued feasibility checking with certified numerical error bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an assignment \(x\), constraints \(C\), and tolerances \(\tau_c\ge0\), compute certified intervals \([\ell_c(x),u_c(x)]\ni v_c(x)\) for every \(c\in C\). Return infeasible if some \(\ell_c(x)>\tau_c\); return feasible if every \(u_c(x)\le\tau_c\); otherwise return unknown and request higher-accuracy evaluation or semantic checking. The output is the first applicable status in this order, together with any constraint attaining it and its certified interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Evaluate certified violation intervals; report infeasible above tolerance, feasible below tolerance, and unknown whenever numerical uncertainty crosses the boundary.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Checking

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three-valued interval procedure is mathematically coherent, but it is a specialized certified-numerics algorithm not supported by the general CP citation and not established as the CIP feasibility-checking interface.

children.title: Semantic–Numerical Checking Boundary
children.top_down_role: Consistency between constraint meaning, tolerances, and candidate acceptance.

assumptions_latex: Exact satisfaction is characterized by \(v_c(x)=0\).
Finite-precision evaluation provides an enclosure \([\ell_c(x),u_c(x)]\ni v_c(x)\) with \(v_c(x)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact infeasibility is certified by \(\ell_c(x)>0\); exact feasibility is certified by \(u_c(x)=0\); all other cases lie on the checking boundary.

notation.meaning: certified numerical enclosure of the violation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between exact semantic certification and tolerance-based numerical classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonnegative exact violation \(v_c(x)\) enclosed by \([\ell_c(x),u_c(x)]\), numerical checking certifies semantic infeasibility when \(\ell_c(x)>0\) and certifies semantic feasibility when \(u_c(x)=0\). If \(0<u_c(x)\) while \(\ell_c(x)\le0\), neither exact conclusion follows. A tolerance decision \(u_c(x)\le\tau_c\) with \(\tau_c>0\) certifies only tolerance-feasibility, not exact satisfaction, unless the declared semantics itself incorporates \(\tau_c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Numerical bounds certify exact semantics only when they separate the violation from zero; tolerance-feasibility is distinct unless tolerance belongs to the semantics.
knowledge_statements.title: Semantic–Numerical Checking Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-separation boundary follows under the stated enclosure model, but neither that certified model nor its role in a CIP handler is supported by the cited CP overview.

children.title: Constraint Resolution Method Pair
children.top_down_role: Handler responses to unresolved relaxation or solution candidates.

children.title: Constraint Enforcement
children.top_down_role: Handler responses that exclude, repair, separate, or reject unresolved candidates.

assumptions_latex: The current relaxation \(R\) contains every feasible solution in the node domain.
A candidate \(\bar x\in R\) violates a handled constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every enforcement response preserves all feasible node solutions while removing \(\bar x\), tightening its domain, or certifying node infeasibility.

notation.meaning: exact feasible set in the node domain

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity-preserving enforcement of a violated handled constraint.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Fundamental concepts and results on polyhedra, linear inequalities, and linear programming p. 85
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a relaxation candidate \(\bar x\in R\setminus F\), an enforcement routine must return one of: a valid inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) satisfying \(F\subseteq\{x:a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\}\) and \(a^{\mathsf T}\bar x>b\); domain reductions valid for every point of \(F\); a certificate that \(F\) is empty in the node domain; or a request for valid branching. Add the cut or reductions and resolve; stop when the candidate satisfies the handled constraint, the node is infeasible, or branching is requested.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Enforcement responds to a violated candidate with a valid cut, valid domain reduction, infeasibility certificate, or request to branch.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Enforcement

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 7. Fundamental concepts and results on polyhedra, linear inequalities, and linear programming p. 85
source_witnesses.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The validity requirements are plausible, but the generic polyhedral and CP sources do not establish this enumeration of CIP constraint-handler enforcement responses or its control flow.

children.title: Constraint Branching
children.top_down_role: Constraint-derived search disjunctions used when direct enforcement is insufficient.

assumptions_latex: The current node has domain \(D\) and exact feasible subset \(F\subseteq D\).
A violating candidate \(\bar x\in D\setminus F\) cannot be resolved adequately by direct enforcement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Valid constraint branching preserves every feasible solution in at least one child and excludes the violating candidate from every child.

notation.meaning: exact feasible subset of the node

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semantics-preserving disjunctive branching generated by a constraint handler.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 1. Disjunctive Programming and Its Relation to Integer Programming p. 1

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a node domain \(D\), feasible subset \(F\), and violating candidate \(\bar x\), construct finitely many child domains \(D_1,\ldots,D_k\) such that \[F\subseteq\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}D_i\subseteq D\quad\text{and}\quad \bar x\notin\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}D_i.\] Optionally require the children to be pairwise disjoint on integer assignments. Replace the node by these children, inherit all valid constraints, and terminate a child when its domain is empty or its relaxation bound proves it irrelevant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint branching creates exhaustive child domains that retain all feasible solutions while excluding the unresolved violating candidate.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint Branching

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 1. Disjunctive Programming and Its Relation to Integer Programming p. 1

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covering and candidate-exclusion conditions describe valid disjunctive branching, but the cited sources do not substantiate this as the specific CIP constraint-handler branching algorithm or its termination rules.

children.title: Enforcement–Branching Selection
children.top_down_role: Structural criteria governing the choice between candidate enforcement and search subdivision.

assumptions_latex: Each admissible enforcement or branching action is validity preserving.
For each action, immediate work and predicted residual search cost are estimated under one fixed model.
