The cited MINLP decomposition locator also does not inspectably support the CP and reusable-explanation specialization. A specialized source is needed before choosing a reliable revision.

children.title: Reusable Justification Regimes
children.top_down_role: Failure and bound structures that admit strong, broadly valid refinements.

children.title: Compact Explanations
children.top_down_role: Small conflict or infeasibility explanations suitable for cross-paradigm translation.

assumptions_latex: \(A\) is a finite set of master literals fixing or restricting the CP subproblem.
The implication represented by \(E\) is valid for the original subproblem predicate \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An infeasibility explanation \(E\) certifies the valid clause \(\bigvee_{\ell\in E}\neg\ell\); a propagation explanation certifies \(\bigvee_{\ell\in E}\neg\ell\vee p\).

notation.meaning: literal justified by a propagation explanation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small subsets of master literals certifying CP-subproblem infeasibility or propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) denote the master variables, let \(z\) denote the CP-subproblem variables, and fix the subproblem predicate \(F(x,z)\) under a finite set \(A\) of master literals. A subset \(E\subseteq A\) is a compact infeasibility explanation when
\[
\bigwedge_{\ell\in E}\ell\Longrightarrow\neg\exists z\;F(x,z),
\]
and its size satisfies a prescribed budget \(|E|\le q\). The clause \(\bigvee_{\ell\in E}\neg\ell\) is then a directly checkable master certificate excluding every master assignment containing \(E\). For a propagated literal \(p\), replace the consequent by \(p\); the valid learned clause becomes \(\bigvee_{\ell\in E}\neg\ell\vee p\). Compactness concerns the number or encoded length of antecedent literals, not merely the runtime used to find them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact explanation uses at most a prescribed number of master literals to entail infeasibility or a propagated literal, yielding a short valid learned clause.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Explanations

children.title: Reusable Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates retaining validity across multiple master states or search contexts.

knowledge_statements.title: Reusable Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound certificates parameterized by interface conditions rather than one complete master assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a parameterized subproblem \(F(u,z)\), a reusable infeasibility certificate is a pair \((R,\pi)\), where \(R(u)\) is an interface predicate and \(\pi\) verifies
\[
\forall u\;\bigl(R(u)\Longrightarrow\neg\exists z\;F(u,z)\bigr).
\]
The master may therefore impose the valid exclusion \(\neg R(u)\). Reuse means that the same verifier and certificate data \(\pi\) establish this implication for every future block or search node whose local model is an instance of the certified template and whose interface parameters satisfy \(R\). A certificate tied only to one complete assignment is reusable only for repetitions of that assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reusable certificate proves infeasibility for every interface parameter satisfying a predicate, allowing the same exclusion to apply across compatible blocks or future search nodes.
assumptions_latex: Every reused subproblem is an instance of the model template certified by \(\pi\).
The interface predicate \(R\) is interpreted identically in the master and certificate verifier.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(R(u)\) holds, \(F(u,z)\) has no feasible completion, so \(\neg R(u)\) is a valid master constraint.

notation.meaning: parameter region covered by the certificate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content kind and parameterized implication fit the terminal, but no source supports the proposed reusable-certificate abstraction, template-instantiation requirement, or cross-node reuse semantics. These are specialized claims and require an inspectable source.

children.title: Certificate Generalization Reach
children.top_down_role: Breadth of assignments, nodes, or subproblems covered by a refinement.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Generalization Reach
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The precisely defined parameter region over which a certificate remains valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a subproblem family \(F(u,z)\) and certificate \(\pi\), define its generalization reach by
\[
\mathcal R(\pi)=\left\{u\in U:\operatorname{Verify}(F,u,\pi)=1\right\}.
\]
For an infeasibility certificate, verifier soundness requires
\[
u\in\mathcal R(\pi)\Longrightarrow\neg\exists z\;F(u,z).
\]
A claimed region \(Q\subseteq U\) is covered exactly when \(Q\subseteq\mathcal R(\pi)\). Its reach is strictly broader than that of \(\pi'\) when \(\mathcal R(\pi')\subsetneq\mathcal R(\pi)\). Reach comparisons are meaningful only for the same parameter universe, subproblem semantics, and sound verifier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate reaches exactly the parameter values accepted by its sound verifier; one certificate generalizes farther when this accepted region strictly contains another's.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is the fixed parameter universe for one subproblem family.
\(\operatorname{Verify}\) is sound for the asserted certificate type.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(u\in\mathcal R(\pi)\) inherits the certified conclusion, and a region \(Q\) is covered precisely if \(Q\subseteq\mathcal R(\pi)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is internally consistent and matches the reach terminal, but it defines a specialized verifier-based notion of certificate generalization without any source. Evidence is required for the accepted-region semantics and reach comparison before candidate-review acceptance.

children.title: Reuse Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Locality or context dependence that prevents broad certificate reuse.

assumptions_latex: \((R,\pi)\) is sound for the original predicate \(F\).
The target predicate \(F'\) may differ from \(F\) in constraints or parameter semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If validity for \(F'\) is not established, \(\neg R(u)\) is not a certified target constraint and must not be reused as such.

notation.meaning: region and certificate proposed for reuse

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which a previously sound subproblem certificate cannot be transferred.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((R,\pi)\) certify \(R(u)\Rightarrow\neg\exists z\;F(u,z)\). Reuse for a target model \(F'(u,z)\) is uncertified whenever the available validation cannot establish
\[
\forall u\;\bigl(R(u)\Longrightarrow\neg\exists z\;F'(u,z)\bigr).
\]
A change to a constraint used by \(\pi\), to the meaning or domain of an interface parameter, or to the relation between \(F\) and \(F'\) is therefore a potential reuse boundary requiring renewed validation; such a change does not by itself prove that reuse is impossible. A target value outside \(R\) is not covered by the original certificate. Without a verified template-preserving mapping or a separate validation for \(F'\), applying \(\neg R(u)\) to the target master is not certified and may exclude a feasible target solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate reuse is uncertified when model semantics, parameter domains, relied-upon constraints, or the covered region change without validation preserving the certified implication; a model change is a reason to revalidate, not by itself proof that transfer is impossible.
knowledge_statements.title: Reuse Failure Boundaries

children.title: Hybrid Inference Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity distinctions governing inference strength, invocation frequency, and state reuse.

children.title: Filtering Effort Regimes
children.top_down_role: Inference-strength regimes distinguished by computational effort and completeness.

children.title: Complete Filtering
children.top_down_role: Filtering regimes pursuing the full targeted consistency level.

knowledge_statements.title: Complete Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact domain-consistency filtering for one finite-domain constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^n U_i\) be a constraint relation and let \(D=(D_1,\ldots,D_n)\), where each \(D_i\subseteq U_i\) is finite. The complete filtering operator for \(R\) is \(F_R(D)=D'\), with
\[
D'_i=\{a\in D_i:\exists x\in R\cap\prod_{j=1}^nD_j\text{ such that }x_i=a\},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]
Thus every retained value has a feasible support within the current domains, and every unsupported value is removed. In particular, \(F_R(D)=D\) exactly when \(D\) is domain consistent for \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Complete filtering removes exactly those domain values having no tuple of the constraint relation compatible with all current domains.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq\prod_{i=1}^n U_i\) is an explicitly or implicitly represented relation.
Each current domain \(D_i\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_R(D)\) is the unique componentwise-largest domain-consistent substore of \(D\).

notation.meaning: Complete filtering operator for the relation.

children.title: Incomplete Filtering
children.top_down_role: Filtering regimes accepting weaker inference than the targeted consistency level.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sound but non-exhaustive filtering relative to complete domain filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the relation \(R\) and domain store \(D\), let \(F_R(D)\) denote complete filtering. A filtering operator \(G_R\) is incomplete at \(D\) when it is contracting and sound,
\[
F_R(D)\subseteq G_R(D)\subseteq D,
\]
but does not attain the complete closure:
\[
G_R(D)\ne F_R(D).
\]
Soundness means that no value belonging to a tuple in \(R\cap\prod_iD_i\) is deleted. Incompleteness therefore consists of retaining at least one value that has no such support.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incomplete filtering is sound and contracting but leaves at least one unsupported value that complete filtering would remove; it need not delete any unsupported value itself.
assumptions_latex: \(R\) is a relation over finite variable domains.
\(G_R\) never removes a value occurring in a currently feasible tuple.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G_R(D)\ne F_R(D)\) while \(F_R(D)\subseteq G_R(D)\subseteq D\).

children.title: Bounded-Effort Filtering
children.top_down_role: Filtering constrained by time, work, depth, or resource budgets.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Effort Filtering
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Anytime sound filtering stopped by an explicit resource budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite domain store \(D^0\), a sound elementary inference oracle \(P\), and a budget \(B\in\mathbb N\). Initialize \(D\leftarrow D^0\) and \(b\leftarrow0\). While \(b<B\), select an unprocessed inference task, apply \(P\) to obtain a sound contraction \(D'\subseteq D\), set \(D\leftarrow D'\), and increment \(b\) by the charged effort. Stop earlier if no task can contract \(D\) or some domain becomes empty. Output \(D\) together with a flag indicating whether the inference queue was exhausted. Queue exhaustion certifies the closure implemented by \(P\); budget exhaustion does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Run sound propagation until its closure, failure, or a fixed effort budget; report whether the resulting store is actually closed.
assumptions_latex: Each oracle contraction preserves every solution in the input store.
Charged effort is nonnegative and the total charge is bounded by \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output preserves all solutions of \(D^0\), uses effort at most \(B\), and need not be propagation-closed when the budget is exhausted.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports this particular budgeted algorithm or effort model. Moreover, testing only that the accumulated charge is below the budget before an inference task does not prevent the next charge from exceeding the budget, and allowing zero charges leaves termination unestablished.

children.title: Filtering Strength Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Navigation across inference yield, invocation cost, plus search impact.

knowledge_statements.title: Filtering Strength Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search reduction and inference cost under nested sound filtering operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_1\) and \(G_2\) be sound, monotone filtering operators such that \(G_2(D)\subseteq G_1(D)\) for every store \(D\); call \(G_2\) at least as strong as \(G_1\). Under the same branching rule, every child store surviving \(G_2\) is contained in the corresponding child store surviving \(G_1\), so stronger filtering cannot create feasible assignments excluded by weaker filtering. Nevertheless, if their per-node costs are \(c_2(D)\) and \(c_1(D)\), neither total runtime \(\sum_D c_k(D)\) nor memory usage is ordered without additional bounds on search-tree reduction and implementation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stronger sound filtering yields smaller stores, but its extra per-node work means that neither total runtime nor memory is automatically better.
assumptions_latex: Both operators are sound and monotone on the same finite-domain stores.
The comparison uses the same branching rule and solution semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Store strength is ordered by \(G_2(D)\subseteq G_1(D)\), whereas total computational cost is not ordered in general.

notation.meaning: Weaker and stronger sound filtering operators.
Cost of applying operator \(G_k\) at store \(D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strength-versus-cost principle fits the leaf, but it has no supporting citation. The child-store comparison also requires a fixed corresponding branching decision or a branching rule invariant under the differing filtered stores.

children.title: Inference Representation Complexity Tradeoff
children.top_down_role: Complexity differences between global reasoning and decomposed representations.

children.title: Global-Constraint Reasoning Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational burden associated with specialized global reasoning.

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Constraint Reasoning Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional hardness of complete filtering for an implicitly represented global constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a family of global relations \(R_I\), indexed by instances \(I\), with finite domains encoded in binary. Define the support problem: given \(I\), a store \(D\), a variable index \(i\), and \(a\in D_i\), decide whether some \(x\in R_I\cap\prod_jD_j\) satisfies \(x_i=a\). If this support problem is NP-complete, then computing complete domain filtering for \(R_I\) is NP-hard, because the filtering output retains \(a\) exactly when the support instance is affirmative. Consequently, no polynomial-time complete filtering algorithm exists for the family unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If deciding whether one value has a support in a global constraint is NP-complete, complete filtering that constraint is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: Global-constraint instances and finite domains have polynomial-length encodings.
The specified value-support decision problem is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complete domain filtering for the family is NP-hard and is not polynomial-time computable unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: Global relation represented by instance I.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conditional reduction is plausible and the complexity-bound kind fits, but no source with an inspectable locator supports the support-problem premise or the resulting NP-hardness formulation.

children.title: Decomposed Representation Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational burden associated with primitive or extended decompositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposed Representation Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size and propagation cost of a primitive constraint decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a global relation on variables \(X\) be represented by primitive constraints \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) over \(X\cup Y\), where \(Y\) contains auxiliary variables and
\[
R=\{x:\exists y\text{ such that }(x,y)\in\bigcap_{k=1}^m C_k\}.
\]
If propagator \(k\) requires time \(t_k\) and storage \(s_k\) per invocation, one full sequential propagation sweep costs \(O(\sum_{k=1}^m t_k)\) time and \(O(\sum_{k=1}^m s_k+|X|+|Y|)\) storage, excluding representation input. Reaching a common fixpoint may require multiple sweeps; projection equivalence alone supplies no polynomial bound on their number or on decomposition size.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decomposition sweep costs the sum of its propagator costs, but equivalent projection alone does not bound decomposition size or fixpoint work.
assumptions_latex: The decomposition is projection-equivalent to \(R\).
Each primitive propagator has stated per-invocation time and storage bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One sweep has additive time and storage bounds, while total closure cost requires an additional bound on invocations or domain contractions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive one-sweep accounting is plausible and appropriately distinguished from fixpoint cost, but the decomposition and storage cost model has no cited source.

children.title: Representation Complexity Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Regimes balancing specialized inference cost against decomposition size or weakness.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Complexity Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tradeoff between compact global representations and expanded primitive decompositions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a global-constraint representation and \(E\) a projection-equivalent decomposition. Compare representation size \(S\), closure time \(T\), and filtering operator \(F\). Compactness and inference strength are independent: \(S(G)<S(E)\) does not imply \(T(G)<T(E)\), and projection equivalence does not imply \(F_G(D)|_X=F_E(D)|_X\). Equality of projected closures requires propagation completeness of \(E\) relative to \(G\). Thus choosing a representation is a multi-criteria decision involving encoding size, propagator complexity, filtering strength, incrementality, and the resulting search tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equivalent compact and decomposed models may differ independently in size, propagation time, filtering strength, reuse, and search performance.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and \(E\) define the same assignments on the original variables \(X\).
Both filtering operators are sound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection equivalence alone orders neither representation size, closure time, nor filtering strength.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the representation-tradeoff leaf, but no citation supports the independence claims or the stated propagation-completeness criterion.

children.title: Decomposition Scalability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Instance structures where decomposed representations become too large or too weak.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Scalability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treewidth boundary for exact inference on a finite-domain decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a decomposed finite-domain constraint network have \(n\) variables, maximum domain size \(d\), and primal-graph treewidth \(w\). Given a width-\(w\) tree decomposition, exact dynamic-programming inference can store tables indexed by at most \(w+1\) variables and run in \(O(n d^{w+1})\) time with \(O(n d^{w+1})\) table space, up to polynomial representation factors. Hence bounded \(w\) and bounded \(d\) yield polynomial scaling in \(n\). If \(w\) grows linearly with \(n\), this bound is exponential even when \(d\ge2\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact inference over a decomposition scales polynomially at bounded treewidth and domain size, but the standard bound becomes exponential when treewidth grows linearly.
assumptions_latex: A width-\(w\) tree decomposition of the primal graph is supplied.
Every variable domain has cardinality at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact table-based inference uses \(O(n d^{w+1})\) time and space up to polynomial representation factors.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-treewidth dynamic-programming boundary is standard and the content kind is appropriate, but the exact time and space exponent requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Incremental Inference Reuse Regimes
children.top_down_role: State-reuse regimes across neighboring nodes, master assignments, or cooperation rounds.

children.title: Incremental Inference Cost
children.top_down_role: Marginal inference effort after a nearby state or assignment change.

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Inference Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Update-sensitive cost of maintaining a propagation fixpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be a propagation fixpoint with maintained state \(S\), and let an update \(\Delta\) monotonically shrink domains. An incremental propagator computes the new fixpoint from \((D,S,\Delta)\). If \(A(\Delta)\) is the multiset of propagator events activated by the update and event \(e\) costs \(c(e)\), its update cost is
\[
T_{\mathrm{inc}}(\Delta)=O\!\left(c_{\mathrm{queue}}+c_{\mathrm{state}}+\sum_{e\in A(\Delta)}c(e)\right).
\]
Incrementality improves the worst-case bound only when the activated-event and state-maintenance terms are asymptotically smaller than recomputation; otherwise \(T_{\mathrm{inc}}\) may equal or exceed full filtering cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Incremental propagation costs the activated inference work plus queue and state maintenance; it helps only when that total is smaller than recomputation.
assumptions_latex: The update \(\Delta\) only removes domain values.
The maintained state remains valid for all unaffected inference events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Incremental cost is governed by activated events and maintenance overhead, with no unconditional advantage over recomputation.

notation.meaning: Inference events activated by the update.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The update-sensitive accounting matches the leaf, but the event multiset, queue overhead, state overhead, and asymptotic comparison are introduced without source support.

children.title: Reusable Inference State
children.top_down_role: Persistent propagator, subproblem, or relaxation state shared across related contexts.

knowledge_statements.title: Reusable Inference State
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cached state sufficient for sound incremental propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a propagator \(P\), a reusable inference state is a summary \(S(D)\) associated with domain store \(D\), together with an update procedure \(U\), such that for every admissible domain contraction \(D'\subseteq D\),
\[
U(S(D),D,D')=S'(D')
\]
and running \(P\) from \(S'(D')\) produces the same sound propagation closure as running \(P\) from a valid freshly constructed state for \(D'\). The summary may contain supports, watched literals, residual graphs, bounds, or queues; its reuse is valid only while the invariants required by \(P\) remain satisfied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reusable inference state is cached information that can be updated after admissible domain changes without altering the propagator's sound closure.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) has explicit state invariants and a well-defined closure.
The update \(D'\subseteq D\) belongs to the state procedure's admissible update class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Updated reusable state yields the same sound closure as valid fresh state for \(D'\).

notation.meaning: Inference summary valid at store D.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition has the correct mathematical role, but no source supports fresh-state equivalence as the defining criterion for reusable propagator state.

children.title: Amortized Reuse Regimes
children.top_down_role: Repeated-solve settings where setup costs spread across many invocations.

knowledge_statements.title: Amortized Reuse Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequence-level criterion for beneficial incremental-state reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(q\) admissible updates \(\Delta_1,\ldots,\Delta_q\). Let \(I\) be initialization cost, \(u_t\) the incremental inference cost after update \(t\), and \(r_t\) the cost of recomputing from fresh state. Reuse has total cost
\[
T_{\mathrm{reuse}}(q)=I+\sum_{t=1}^q u_t
\]
and amortized cost \(I/q+q^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^q u_t\). It is beneficial over repeated recomputation exactly when \(I+\sum_tu_t<\sum_tr_t\). If \(I=o(\sum_tr_t)\) and \(\sum_tu_t=o(\sum_tr_t)\), reuse provides an asymptotic improvement; otherwise only constant-factor or no improvement follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: State reuse helps over an update sequence precisely when initialization plus incremental costs are below the sum of fresh recomputation costs.
assumptions_latex: All updates preserve the invariants needed by reusable state unless an invalidation cost is charged.
Costs are measured under the same computational model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reuse is advantageous exactly when \(I+\sum_{t=1}^q u_t<\sum_{t=1}^q r_t\).

notation.meaning: Fresh recomputation cost at update t.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequence-level cost comparison is algebraically coherent and fits a complexity-bound leaf, but it lacks a source for the computational model and asymptotic reuse criterion.

children.title: State Invalidation Costs
children.top_down_role: Reconstruction burden caused by changes that invalidate retained inference state.

knowledge_statements.title: State Invalidation Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost consequence when updates violate cached-state invariants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be reusable state whose validity predicate at store \(D\) is \(V(S,D)\). For an update producing \(D'\), if \(V(S,D')\) fails and no repair procedure restores it, sound incremental inference must discard or rebuild the invalid portion before reuse. Writing \(J(\Delta)\) for invalidation detection and repair cost, the update cost becomes
\[
T(\Delta)=J(\Delta)+T_{\mathrm{inc}}(\Delta).
\]
If invalidation forces complete rebuilding with cost \(R(D')\), then \(J(\Delta)=\Omega(R(D'))\); repeated such updates eliminate any asymptotic benefit that depended on retaining \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When an update breaks cached-state invariants, detection and repair or rebuilding must be charged, and repeated rebuilding can erase reuse benefits.
assumptions_latex: State is used only while its validity predicate holds.
Invalid state cannot be consumed soundly without repair or reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Invalidation adds \(J(\Delta)\) to update cost, and full rebuilding gives \(J(\Delta)=\Omega(R(D'))\).

notation.meaning: Validity predicate for state at a domain store.
Cost of rebuilding state at the updated store.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the invalidation-cost leaf, but the additive cost model and the claimed rebuilding lower bound have no supporting citation or inspectable locator.

children.title: Hybrid Scalability Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Performance failures caused by duplicated state, translation, excessive inference, or model growth.

children.title: Replicated-State Overhead
children.top_down_role: Memory, maintenance, and communication costs of multiple solver representations.

children.title: Duplicated State Footprint
children.top_down_role: Memory or representation growth from maintaining multiple solver views.

knowledge_statements.title: Duplicated State Footprint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Memory accounting for replicated hybrid-solver state.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\ge 1\) solver components each retain a copy of shared state of size \(S\) bytes, and let component \(r\) additionally retain private state of size \(P_r\) bytes. The aggregate state footprint is \[M_R=RS+\sum_{r=1}^{R}P_r.\] Relative to one shared copy plus all private states, the duplicated-state overhead is \[D_R=M_R-\left(S+\sum_{r=1}^{R}P_r\right)=(R-1)S.\] Thus any fixed positive shared-state size produces memory overhead linear in the replica count.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replicating shared state across R solver components adds exactly (R−1) copies, so the duplicated memory grows linearly with the number of replicas.
assumptions_latex: \(R\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}\).
\(S\ge 0\) and \(P_r\ge 0\) are measured without double-counting.

notation.meaning: number of solver components holding replicas

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct additive memory accounting for replicated data

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The additive memory accounting is precise and fits a representation of duplicated-state footprint, but no inspectable citation supports its use for replicated hybrid-solver state.

children.title: Synchronization Traffic
children.top_down_role: Data movement required to keep solver representations aligned.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Traffic
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Communication volume generated by replicated-state updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: During a horizon \([0,T]\), let update \(j\) have encoded size \(b_j\) bytes and be transmitted to \(f_j\) replica destinations. Excluding acknowledgments and protocol headers, synchronization traffic is \[B_{\mathrm{sync}}(T)=\sum_{j=1}^{U(T)}f_jb_j.\] If every update has size at least \(b>0\) and is broadcast from one origin to all other \(R-1\) replicas, then \[B_{\mathrm{sync}}(T)\ge (R-1)bU(T).\] Hence synchronization volume scales at least linearly in both update count and replica count under full broadcast.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Synchronization traffic equals update size times destination fan-out; full broadcast yields traffic at least linear in updates and replicas.
assumptions_latex: \(U(T)<\infty\) counts state updates issued by time \(T\).
Each destination transmission is counted once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{sync}}(T)=\sum_{j=1}^{U(T)}f_jb_j\), with \(B_{\mathrm{sync}}(T)\ge(R-1)bU(T)\) under full broadcast.

notation.meaning: number of updates through time T
number of destinations receiving update j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: message-volume accounting by payload and fan-out

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The payload-by-fan-out accounting is internally correct and the representation kind fits, but the record has no source with a specific locator.

children.title: Consistency Maintenance Cost
children.top_down_role: Processing effort spent reconciling updates across duplicated states.

knowledge_statements.title: Consistency Maintenance Cost
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Work required to keep solver replicas mutually consistent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For synchronization events \(j=1,\ldots,U\), let \(c_j^{\mathrm{enc}}\), \(c_j^{\mathrm{net}}\), \(c_j^{\mathrm{apply}}\), and \(c_j^{\mathrm{wait}}\) denote encoding, communication, replica-update, and consistency-wait costs. Define total consistency-maintenance cost by \[C_{\mathrm{cons}}(U)=\sum_{j=1}^{U}\left(c_j^{\mathrm{enc}}+c_j^{\mathrm{net}}+c_j^{\mathrm{apply}}+c_j^{\mathrm{wait}}\right).\] If each event requires at least \(c_{min}>0\) total work, then \(C_{\mathrm{cons}}(U)\ge Uc_{min}\); consistency therefore imposes an unavoidable cost proportional to the number of synchronization events.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Consistency cost aggregates encoding, communication, update, and waiting costs and is at least linear in synchronization events when each event has positive cost.
assumptions_latex: All component costs are nonnegative.
\(U\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{cons}}(U)\ge Uc_{min}\) whenever every event costs at least \(c_{min}>0\).

notation.meaning: cost components of synchronization event j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive decomposition of consistency overhead

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed bound follows from the stipulated additive cost model, but no cited source supports that decomposition or its architectural interpretation.

children.title: Synchronization Scalability Limits
children.top_down_role: Problem scales or update frequencies where synchronization dominates useful solving work.

knowledge_statements.title: Synchronization Scalability Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity boundary beyond which replicated-state synchronization cannot maintain a uniformly bounded backlog.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose updates have long-run arrival rate \(\lambda\), each update generates \(f\) destination messages of mean size \(b\), and the synchronization subsystem can provide at most sustained message and byte service rates \(\mu\) and \(C\), respectively. If \[\lambda f>\mu\quad\text{or}\quad \lambda fb>C,\] then, absent update dropping or coalescing, cumulative synchronization demand exceeds cumulative service by an amount growing linearly with time, so the backlog cannot remain uniformly bounded. Equality with a capacity is boundary behavior and requires additional arrival and service assumptions before boundedness or instability can be concluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict overload of either message-processing or byte-transfer capacity makes an undropped, uncoalesced synchronization backlog unbounded; equality is inconclusive without a more detailed queueing model.
assumptions_latex: \(\lambda,f,b,\mu,C\ge 0\).
Cumulative arrival demand and available service admit the stated long-run rates.
Updates are neither dropped nor coalesced.
\(\mu\) and \(C\) are upper bounds on sustained service rates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\lambda f>\mu\) or \(\lambda fb>C\), the synchronization backlog cannot remain uniformly bounded.

children.title: Expensive Low-Yield Inference
children.top_down_role: Propagation or subproblem work whose search impact does not justify its cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive Low-Yield Inference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational criterion for inference whose search benefit is too small.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an inference action \(a\) at search state \(s\), let \(c(a,s)>0\) be its computational cost and let \(g(a,s)\ge0\) be a specified measurable search gain, such as nodes avoided, bound improvement, or domain reduction. Given an admissible gain-per-cost threshold \(\tau>0\), the action is expensive low-yield precisely when \[\frac{\mathbb{E}[g(a,s)]}{\mathbb{E}[c(a,s)]}<\tau,\] where expectations use the declared distribution of comparable search states. The gain definition and threshold must be fixed before comparing inference mechanisms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inference is expensive low-yield when its expected measurable search gain per unit expected cost falls below a predetermined threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\mathbb{E}[c(a,s)]<\infty\).
\(0\le\mathbb{E}[g(a,s)]<\infty\).
The gain metric and comparison distribution are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\) is expensive low-yield at threshold \(\tau\) if and only if \(\mathbb{E}[g(a,s)]/\mathbb{E}[c(a,s)]<\tau\).

notation.meaning: computational cost of inference action a at state s
declared search gain from the action
minimum acceptable expected gain per unit cost

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is mathematically well-defined and matches the node role, but the gain metric, reference distribution, and threshold are architecture-dependent and have no supporting source.

children.title: Hybrid Model Growth Failures
children.top_down_role: Growth caused by excessive cuts, translated constraints, or auxiliary variables.

children.title: Cut-Pool Growth
children.top_down_role: Accumulation of generated refinements with declining marginal pruning value.

knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Pool Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size growth of a retained pool of generated cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{P}_t\) be the cut pool after iteration \(t\), let \(A_t\) be the cuts admitted at that iteration, and let \(D_t\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{t-1}\) be the cuts deleted before admission. Then \[|\mathcal{P}_t|=|\mathcal{P}_{t-1}|-|D_t|+|A_t|.\] Consequently, \[|\mathcal{P}_T|=|\mathcal{P}_0|+\sum_{t=1}^{T}\bigl(|A_t|-|D_t|\bigr).\] If at least \(q>0\) net cuts are retained per iteration, then \(|\mathcal{P}_T|\ge|\mathcal{P}_0|+qT\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cut-pool size equals its initial size plus admitted cuts minus deleted cuts; positive net retention causes at least linear growth.
assumptions_latex: Each admitted cut is distinct from cuts retained immediately before admission.
\(D_t\subseteq\mathcal{P}_{t-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal{P}_T|=|\mathcal{P}_0|+\sum_{t=1}^{T}(|A_t|-|D_t|)\).

notation.meaning: retained cut pool after iteration t
previously retained cuts deleted at iteration t

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact set-cardinality accounting for cut retention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cut-pool cardinality identity is correct under the stated distinctness and deletion assumptions, and representation is an appropriate kind, but no cut-management source is cited.

children.title: Master-Model Growth
children.top_down_role: Expansion of the master through translated constraints, states, or auxiliaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Master-Model Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cumulative growth of a decomposition master formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a master formulation initially contain \(n_0\) variables and \(m_0\) constraints. At iteration \(t\), suppose \(v_t\) variables and \(r_t\) constraints are added, while \(\bar v_t\) variables and \(\bar r_t\) constraints are removed. After \(T\) iterations its dimensions are \[n_T=n_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}(v_t-\bar v_t),\qquad m_T=m_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}(r_t-\bar r_t).\] Without deletion, uniformly positive additions make at least one master dimension grow linearly with \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A master model’s dimensions equal initial dimensions plus cumulative additions minus removals; persistent additions without deletion cause linear growth.
assumptions_latex: All dimension increments are nonnegative integers.
Every removal concerns an object present in the current master.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(n_T=n_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}(v_t-\bar v_t)\) and \(m_T=m_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}(r_t-\bar r_t)\).

notation.meaning: numbers of master variables and constraints after T iterations
variables and constraints added at iteration t
variables and constraints removed at iteration t

children.title: Relaxation Expansion
children.top_down_role: Growth of relaxation representations used for bounding or cross-solver exchange.

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension expansion caused by accumulated relaxation components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the initial relaxation be \(R_0=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n_0}:A_0x\le b_0\}\), where \(A_0\) has \(m_0\) rows. Suppose iteration \(t\) adds \(v_t\) auxiliary variables and \(r_t\) valid inequalities without removing earlier components. After \(T\) iterations, the explicit relaxation has \[n_T=n_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}v_t,\qquad m_T=m_0+\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_t\] variables and inequalities. Expansion may strengthen the projection onto the original variables, while the explicit algebraic representation grows by exactly the accumulated additions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from n₀ variables and m₀ inequalities, adding auxiliary variables and valid inequalities without deletion increases the explicit relaxation dimensions by their cumulative counts, even if projection onto the original variables becomes stronger.
assumptions_latex: \(A_0\) has exactly \(m_0\) rows.
\(v_t,r_t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\) for \(t=1,\ldots,T\).
All added inequalities are valid for the intended feasible set.
No previously present variable or inequality is removed.

notation.meaning: initial numbers of variables and inequalities
auxiliary variables added at iteration t
valid inequalities added at iteration t
numbers of variables and inequalities after T iterations

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact dimension accounting under monotone formulation expansion

children.title: Bloat-Induced Performance Loss
children.top_down_role: Memory, reoptimization, separation, or numerical costs caused by excessive model growth.

knowledge_statements.title: Bloat-Induced Performance Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: When model growth costs more than the search it saves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T_0(N)\) be runtime with a fixed baseline model for an instance of scale \(N\). For an expanded model, let \(H_N\ge0\) be additional construction and maintenance time, \(S_N\ge0\) the search time saved by stronger inference, and \(Q_N\ge0\) the additional time spent solving enlarged relaxations or subproblems. Its runtime difference is \[T_{\mathrm{exp}}(N)-T_0(N)=H_N+Q_N-S_N.\] Bloat-induced performance loss occurs exactly when \(H_N+Q_N>S_N\), in which case expansion increases total runtime despite any search reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model bloat hurts performance exactly when construction, maintenance, and enlarged-solve overhead exceed the search time saved by stronger inference.
assumptions_latex: Both configurations solve the same instance to the same stopping criterion.
Runtime is partitioned consistently into the displayed components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{exp}}(N)>T_0(N)\) if and only if \(H_N+Q_N>S_N\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: runtime difference decomposed into overhead and savings

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure boundary is correct under the stipulated exhaustive runtime partition and fits the terminal container, but no solver-performance source supports the decomposition.

children.title: Cross-Solver Coupling Failures
children.top_down_role: Architectures retaining strong coupling or exchanging information with little pruning value.

children.title: Residual Cross-Solver Coupling
children.top_down_role: Strong dependencies left unresolved by the chosen solver partition.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Cross-Solver Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling remaining after partitioning a hybrid optimization model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the model entities among solver components \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\), and form an interaction graph \(G=(V,E)\), where an edge joins entities that occur together in a constraint, objective term, or required inference. The partition has residual cross-solver coupling precisely when \[E_{\mathrm{cross}}=\{\{u,v\}\in E:u\in V_i, v\in V_j, i\ne j\}\ne\varnothing.\] Each edge in \(E_{\mathrm{cross}}\) represents information that cannot be evaluated entirely within one component and therefore requires communication, duplication, or a coordinating consistency mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual coupling exists when at least one model interaction crosses solver partitions, requiring communication, duplication, or coordination.
assumptions_latex: \(V_1,\ldots,V_k\) are pairwise disjoint and cover \(V\).
Graph edges encode all interactions relevant to solver correctness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual cross-solver coupling holds if and only if \(E_{\mathrm{cross}}\ne\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: entities assigned to solver component i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: graph-cut characterization of partition coupling

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-cut condition is coherent and matches residual coupling, but its claim that all cross edges require communication, duplication, or coordination depends on the chosen interaction graph and needs a hybrid-partitioning source.

children.title: Unbalanced Solver Partitions
children.top_down_role: Work allocations that overload one solver or underuse complementary capabilities.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbalanced Solver Partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Execution-time imbalance criterion for hybrid solver partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k\ge2\) solver partitions, let \(W_i>0\) be the predicted or measured execution time of partition \(i\) over a fixed reference horizon under a fixed resource assignment and cost model. Define mean partition time \(\bar W=k^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{k}W_i\) and imbalance factor \[I=\frac{\max_{1\le i\le k}W_i}{\bar W}.\] For a prescribed tolerance \(\beta\ge1\), the partition is unbalanced when \(I>\beta\). If a barrier waits for every partition, the barrier completion time is at least \(\max_i W_i=I\bar W\), so the slowest partition determines this lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solver partitioning is unbalanced when its largest partition execution time exceeds a chosen multiple of the mean; a barrier cannot complete before that slowest partition finishes.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge2}\) and \(W_i>0\) for every \(i\).
All \(W_i\) use the same reference horizon, resource assignment, and time unit.
Barrier completion waits for every partition.
\(\beta\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partition is unbalanced at tolerance \(\beta\) exactly when \(I>\beta\), and barrier completion time is at least \(I\bar W\).

notation.meaning: execution time of solver partition i

children.title: Low-Value Feedback
children.top_down_role: Exchanged information yielding little pruning, bounding, or feasibility progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Value Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feedback whose solver benefit does not justify transfer cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For feedback message \(m\) sent from one solver component to another, let \(v(m)\ge0\) be its expected reduction in recipient search cost and let \(c(m)>0\) be its communication, translation, validation, and integration cost, all measured in a common unit. Given threshold \(\tau>0\), feedback is low-value when \[\frac{\mathbb{E}[v(m)]}{\mathbb{E}[c(m)]}<\tau.\] A stream \(M\) is collectively detrimental under the additive model when \(\sum_{m\in M}\mathbb{E}[v(m)]<\sum_{m\in M}\mathbb{E}[c(m)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feedback is low-value when expected recipient search savings per unit transfer-and-integration cost fall below a fixed threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(0<\mathbb{E}[c(m)]<\infty\).
\(0\le\mathbb{E}[v(m)]<\infty\).
Costs and benefits use a common unit and fixed reference distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Message \(m\) is low-value at threshold \(\tau\) if and only if \(\mathbb{E}[v(m)]/\mathbb{E}[c(m)]<\tau\).

notation.meaning: recipient search cost saved by feedback message m
total transfer and integration cost of message m

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: expected benefit-to-cost criterion for exchanged information

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The benefit-to-cost condition is internally consistent and appropriate as a condition, but its value model and additive stream criterion are architecture-dependent and unsupported by an inspectable citation.

children.title: Delayed Feedback
children.top_down_role: Useful cross-solver information arriving too late to influence the relevant search context.

knowledge_statements.title: Delayed Feedback
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for asynchronous information exchange between coupled master and subordinate solvers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_k\) be the master relaxation at iteration \(k\), and let feedback \(F_k\) be derived from subordinate-solver state \(s_k\) with validity region \(V_k\). If \(F_k\) is installed only at iteration \(k+d\), where \(d>0\), then its use is sound only if every master point affected by \(F_k\) belongs to \(V_k\). Delayed-feedback failure occurs when a point \(x\in R_{k+d}\setminus V_k\) is rejected or certified using \(F_k\); delay is merely a scalability failure when \(F_k\) remains valid but arrives after the search has explored nodes it would have pruned.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delayed feedback is incorrect if applied outside its original validity region; it is only inefficient when still valid but received after avoidable search has occurred.
assumptions_latex: \(F_k\) depends on subordinate state \(s_k\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in R_{k+d}\setminus V_k\) must not be rejected or certified using \(F_k\).
review_flags: hybrid-specific formalization requires an authoritative source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation or locator supports this hybrid-specific validity formulation. The record also blends correctness failure from out-of-scope feedback with the scalability sense required by its placement under Hybrid Scalability Failure Taxonomy.

children.title: Hybrid Correctness Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Failure modes threatening correctness of enforcement, pruning, cuts, certificates, or bounds.

children.title: Incomplete Constraint Enforcement
children.top_down_role: Failure to cover relevant relaxation and candidate-solution regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Constraint Enforcement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary requiring enforcement across both relaxation and candidate-solution regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the solver's search domain and let the intended feasible set be \(F=\{x\in X:C_i(x)\text{ holds for every }i\in I\}\). Suppose enforcement procedures are invoked only on regimes \(E_i\subseteq X\) for constraint \(C_i\). Enforcement is complete only if every point that can be accepted, used to bound, or returned lies in each relevant \(E_i\), and acceptance implies \(C_i(x)\) for all \(i\in I\). Incomplete enforcement occurs if some reachable \(x\notin F\) can be accepted or certified because at least one violated constraint is not checked in that regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint enforcement is incomplete when a reachable infeasible point can be accepted, bounded from, or returned because a relevant constraint is not checked there.
assumptions_latex: \(F=\{x\in X:C_i(x)\text{ for all }i\in I\}\)
Acceptance and bounding regimes are specified
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x\in X\setminus F\) reachable and accepted without checking some violated \(C_i\) implies incomplete enforcement.

notation.meaning: regimes where constraint i is enforced

review_flags: no supplied locator directly supports hybrid enforcement completeness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No cited source supports the proposed completeness criterion. The plain statement includes bounding from an infeasible point, while the formal failure condition only covers acceptance or certification, so the claimed regimes are not fully aligned.

children.title: Invalid Cut or Certificate Generalization
children.top_down_role: Reuse beyond the master domain or search context justified by the originating inference.

knowledge_statements.title: Invalid Cut or Certificate Generalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for reusing contextual inferences beyond their originating domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D_s\) be the master domain represented by search context \(s\), and let an inference \(g(x)\leq 0\) satisfy \(g(x)\leq0\) for every feasible \(x\in D_s\). Reusing it in context \(t\) is sound only if every feasible point in \(D_t\) also satisfies the inequality, or if its installation is restricted to \(D_s\cap D_t\). Invalid generalization occurs when there exists a feasible \(\bar x\in D_t\setminus D_s\) with \(g(\bar x)>0\), because the reused cut or certificate then excludes a feasible point or supports an unjustified conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contextual cut or certificate is generalized invalidly when reused in a broader context containing a feasible point that violates the inference.
assumptions_latex: \(g(x)\leq0\) is established only for feasible points in \(D_s\)
Context \(t\) may have domain \(D_t\not\subseteq D_s\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\bar x\in D_t\setminus D_s\) feasible with \(g(\bar x)>0\) makes unrestricted reuse unsound.

notation.meaning: domains associated with source and target contexts

review_flags: contextual-validity formulation lacks a directly supporting supplied source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and contextual-validity formulation fit the leaf, but no source or inspectable locator supports extending the same condition from cuts to certificates.

children.title: Solver Context Consistency Failures
children.top_down_role: Mismatch among transformed models, node-local state, and retained plugin data.

children.title: Stale Node-Local Information
children.top_down_role: Retained local data used outside its valid search-node context.

knowledge_statements.title: Stale Node-Local Information
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for information cached at a branch-and-bound node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let node \(u\) have local domain \(D_u\), solver state version \(v_u\), and cached inference \(q_u\) valid under both. At a later node or revised state \((w,v_w)\), using \(q_u\) is sound only if its validity predicate \(P(q_u,D_w,v_w)\) holds. Stale-information failure occurs when \(P(q_u,D_w,v_w)\) is false but \(q_u\) is nevertheless used to prune, propagate, bound, or certify. In particular, ancestry alone is insufficient when model transformations, local bounds, tolerances, or subordinate-solver state have changed dependencies of \(q_u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node-local information becomes stale when its domain or state dependencies change, yet it is still used for pruning, propagation, bounding, or certification.
assumptions_latex: \(q_u\) has explicit domain and state dependencies
The solver may revise state after creating node \(u\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\neg P(q_u,D_w,v_w)\) forbids correctness-critical use of \(q_u\) at state \((w,v_w)\).
review_flags: solver-state validity claim needs implementation-independent sourcing

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement fits the solver-context failure leaf, but the implementation-independent validity predicate and claims about changed dependencies have no cited authoritative support.

children.title: Transformed-Model Drift
children.top_down_role: Mismatch between plugin data and the solver's current transformed representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Transformed-Model Drift
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency boundary between evolving transformed models and original-model semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be an original model and \(T_v(M)\) its transformed representation at version \(v\), with semantic map \(\phi_v\) from transformed solutions to original variables. An inference \(h_v(y)\leq0\) created for \(T_v(M)\) may be used at version \(w\) only after a validity-preserving transport through the maps \(\phi_v\) and \(\phi_w\). Transformed-model drift occurs if the solver applies the unchanged inference to \(T_w(M)\) although some feasible \(y\) of \(T_w(M)\) has \(h_v(y)>0\), or if reported transformed solutions no longer map to solutions satisfying \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model drift occurs when transformations change but old inferences or solution mappings are used without a validity-preserving translation.
assumptions_latex: \(T_v(M)\) and \(T_w(M)\) may use different variables or reductions
\(\phi_v\) and \(\phi_w\) define original-model semantics
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Untransported use of \(h_v\) is unsound whenever it excludes a feasible point of \(T_w(M)\).
review_flags: no supplied source addresses transformed-model version consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation supports this transformed-model versioning criterion. Moreover, maps from transformed solutions to original variables do not by themselves establish a validity-preserving transport of an inequality between transformed variable spaces.

children.title: Callback Context Inconsistency
children.top_down_role: Information accessed or applied in an incompatible callback context.

knowledge_statements.title: Callback Context Inconsistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness boundary for context-sensitive callbacks in a hybrid solver.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a callback invocation expose context \(c=(D,z,b,v)\), comprising the current local domain, relaxation point, bound information, and model version. A callback response \(r(c)\) may modify the search only when its precondition \(Q(c)\) holds and its claimed validity scope contains the installation context. Callback context inconsistency occurs if the response is computed from a different context \(c'\), if required fields are unavailable or transient, or if a local response is installed globally. It becomes correctness-critical whenever the inconsistent response prunes a feasible solution, changes a valid bound, or certifies acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A callback is context-inconsistent when it reads one solver state or validity scope but its response is applied as though produced for another.
assumptions_latex: The callback declares a precondition and validity scope
Callback responses can affect search correctness
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(Q(c)\) fails or the installation context exceeds the response scope, correctness-critical application of \(r(c)\) is invalid.
review_flags: callback semantics are solver-dependent and need authoritative documentation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but callback fields, availability, response scope, and installation semantics are solver-dependent and lack authoritative documentation or a locator.

children.title: Plugin-State Invalidation
children.top_down_role: Retained extension state surviving model, node, or restart changes that revoke its validity.

knowledge_statements.title: Plugin-State Invalidation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependency-based invalidation criterion for stateful hybrid-solver plugins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a plugin cache state \(p\) computed from dependencies \(\Delta(p)\), including model version, node domain, parameters, tolerances, or subordinate-solver state. After a transition from solver state \(s\) to \(s'\), the cache remains usable only if every dependency in \(\Delta(p)\) has unchanged semantics or \(p\) has been recomputed by a valid update map. Plugin-state invalidation failure occurs when a changed dependency is not detected and stale \(p\) influences propagation, separation, branching, bounding, or certification. If \(p\) is used only heuristically, the failure may affect performance rather than correctness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Plugin state is invalid after an unhandled dependency change; using it can corrupt correctness-critical decisions or, if purely heuristic, only degrade performance.
assumptions_latex: Plugin state \(p\) has identifiable dependencies \(\Delta(p)\)
Solver transitions may change dependency semantics
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A changed dependency without valid recomputation forbids correctness-critical use of \(p\).

notation.meaning: solver states before and after a transition

review_flags: plugin lifecycle and invalidation semantics need an authoritative source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dependency-based invalidation account fits the leaf, but no source establishes the assumed plugin lifecycle, update-map semantics, or correctness-versus-performance distinction.

children.title: Numerical–Logical Semantic Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Disagreement between floating-point decisions and discrete constraint semantics.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical–Logical Semantic Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between tolerance-based numerical predicates and exact discrete semantics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a numerical component declare \(a(x)\leq b\) satisfied when \(a(x)\leq b+\varepsilon\), while a logical component interprets the same constraint exactly and treats an integer variable as integral only when it belongs to \(\mathbb Z\). A semantic mismatch exists if the components can assign different truth values to the same exchanged state. It is correctness-critical when some \(x\) with \(b<a(x)\leq b+\varepsilon\), or some nonintegral value accepted by an integrality tolerance, is logically certified feasible or used to derive an inference requiring exact satisfaction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical–logical mismatch occurs when tolerance-based and exact components disagree on feasibility or integrality, enabling an invalid logical conclusion.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\) is a numerical feasibility tolerance
Logical inference requires exact constraint or integrality semantics
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Different truth values for an exchanged state prohibit exact logical certification from the tolerant numerical decision alone.
review_flags: exact hybrid tolerance interface requires direct source support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind matches the leaf, but the exact interface between tolerant numerical decisions and logical certification needs direct support. The domain of x and the function a are also not explicitly specified.

children.title: Logic-Based Decomposition Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structures that weaken master refinement, destabilize subproblems, or prevent exact certification.

children.title: Limited-Reach Cut Regimes
children.top_down_role: Refinements eliminating little beyond already tested master states.

children.title: Assignment-Specific Cuts
children.top_down_role: Refinements tied closely to a single tested master assignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment-Specific Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No-good cut representation excluding one binary master assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For binary master variables \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\), let \(\bar x\in\{0,1\}^n\) be an assignment proved infeasible by a subordinate problem. The assignment-specific no-good cut is \[\sum_{i:\bar x_i=0}x_i+\sum_{i:\bar x_i=1}(1-x_i)\geq1.\] The left-hand side equals zero exactly at \(x=\bar x\), so the cut excludes that assignment and no other binary assignment. It is valid whenever infeasibility has been established for the complete assignment \(\bar x\), but its pruning reach is one assignment unless additional structure supports a stronger generalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The binary no-good cut excludes exactly one infeasible assignment, making it valid but minimally general unless further conflict structure is available.
assumptions_latex: The complete assignment \(\bar x\) is infeasible
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequality holds for every binary \(x\neq\bar x\) and fails exactly at \(x=\bar x\).
review_flags: standard no-good cut formula lacks a directly matching supplied locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind, binary no-good-cut formula, and exact single-assignment exclusion claim are mathematically consistent, but the record supplies no citation or locator as required.

children.title: Weakly Generalized Cuts
children.top_down_role: Refinements extending beyond one assignment while retaining narrow validity or impact.

knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Generalized Cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pruning boundary for valid cuts capturing only a small subset of an infeasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the discrete master domain, \(B\subseteq X\) the assignments whose subordinate problems are infeasible, and \(c(x)\leq0\) a valid cut. Define its exclusion set by \(E_c=\{x\in X:c(x)>0\}\). The cut is weakly generalized relative to \(B\) when \(E_c\subseteq B\) but \(E_c\) covers only a small fraction of \(B\), for example \(|E_c|/|B|\leq\rho\) for a specified \(0<\rho\ll1\). Correctness is preserved, but repeated subordinate solves remain necessary for points in \(B\setminus E_c\), limiting scalability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly generalized cut is valid but excludes only a small portion of the infeasible master assignments, leaving most similar failures undiscovered.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(B\) are finite
\(E_c\subseteq B\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|E_c|/|B|\leq\rho\), then at least \((1-\rho)|B|\) infeasible assignments remain unexcluded.
review_flags: coverage criterion is a local formalization requiring literature support

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coverage-ratio definition is a local, nonstandard formalization without a source. It also requires B to be nonempty for |E_c|/|B| to be defined.

children.title: Limited Pruning Reach
children.top_down_role: Search regions left unaffected by narrowly scoped decomposition refinements.

knowledge_statements.title: Limited Pruning Reach
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Iteration lower bound induced by cuts with uniformly bounded exclusion reach.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a finite set of infeasible master assignments encountered by a decomposition method. Suppose each subordinate solve generates a valid cut excluding at most \(r\) previously unexcluded members of \(B\), where \(r\geq1\). Any procedure relying solely on such cuts requires at least \(\lceil |B|/r\rceil\) generated cuts, and hence at least that many subordinate-solver calls, to exclude all of \(B\). Consequently, if \(|B|\) grows exponentially with the master dimension while \(r\) grows polynomially, this cut mechanism alone has an exponential worst-case call requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every generated cut removes at most r new bad assignments, excluding B needs at least ceiling(|B|/r) subordinate calls and may be exponential.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is finite
Each generated cut excludes at most \(r\) new elements of \(B\)
One subordinate call generates at most one such cut
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least \(\lceil |B|/r\rceil\) subordinate-solver calls are required to exclude all assignments in \(B\).

notation.meaning: maximum number of newly excluded assignments per cut

review_flags: elementary counting bound is unsourced in the supplied inventory

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind correctly fits the terminal container, and the counting bound follows under the stated one-cut-per-call assumptions, but no citation or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Repeated-State Exclusion
children.top_down_role: Decomposition behavior dominated by excluding tested states with little broader master improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-State Exclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of exact-state no-good cuts under redundant or equivalent master encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the master state space and let \(\sim\) denote equivalence of states that induce the same subordinate problem. After failure at \(\bar x\in X\), exact repeated-state exclusion installs a constraint whose exclusion set is \(\{\bar x\}\). This prevents reevaluation of \(\bar x\) but does not prevent evaluation of any distinct \(x\sim\bar x\). If the equivalence class \([\bar x]\) has cardinality \(m\), exact-state cuts may require up to \(m\) subordinate failures to eliminate that single induced problem. Excluding all of \([\bar x]\) is valid only when equivalence and shared infeasibility are certified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact-state cut prevents one repeated assignment but may leave many equivalent encodings of the same failing subordinate problem available.
assumptions_latex: \(\sim\) preserves the induced subordinate problem
\(\bar x\) induces an infeasible subordinate problem
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A cut excluding only \(\bar x\) leaves every state in \([\bar x]\setminus\{\bar x\}\) available for repeated evaluation.

notation.meaning: equivalence class of the failed state

review_flags: equivalence-class failure mechanism needs a direct decomposition source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-state exclusion conclusion fits the leaf, but the equivalence-class mechanism lacks a cited decomposition source. The claim about requiring up to m subordinate failures also needs an explicit search assumption governing whether all equivalent states are evaluated.

children.title: Expensive, Unstable, or Nonincremental Subproblems
children.top_down_role: Subproblem regimes that dominate decomposition cost or defeat state reuse.

knowledge_statements.title: Expensive, Unstable, or Nonincremental Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational boundary for repeated subproblem solution in logic-based decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^k\in X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be successive master decisions, let \(T_0(x^k)>0\) be cold-start subproblem time, and let \(T(s^{k-1},x^k)\) be time using retained state \(s^{k-1}\). The subproblem regime is expensive if \[\frac{\sum_{k=1}^N T(s^{k-1},x^k)}{T_M(N)+\sum_{k=1}^N T(s^{k-1},x^k)}\longrightarrow 1,\] where \(T_M(N)\) is cumulative master time. It is unstable if some sequence satisfying \(\lVert x^k-x^{k-1}\rVert\to0\) has \(T(s^{k-1},x^k)/T_0(x^k)\to\infty\). It is nonincremental along the sequence if \(T(s^{k-1},x^k)/T_0(x^k)\to1\). Any of these conditions removes the expected computational advantage of repeated decomposed solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The viability boundary is crossed when subproblems dominate runtime, warm starts become arbitrarily harmful under small changes, or retained state yields asymptotically no savings.
assumptions_latex: \(T_0(x)>0\) for every evaluated \(x\in X\).
The master and subproblem times are measured under a fixed computational protocol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least one displayed regime prevents asymptotically effective reuse of decomposed subproblem computation.

notation.meaning: Cold-start solution time for the subproblem at master decision x.
Subproblem solution time when retained state s is supplied.
Cumulative master-processing time through iteration N.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The runtime ratios are bespoke operational definitions with no citation. Moreover, subproblem-time dominance alone does not imply ineffective state reuse, so the final claim is not established by the displayed conditions.

children.title: Master-Recourse Guidance Failures
children.top_down_role: Insufficient master guidance or unreliable representation of subproblem contributions.

children.title: Weak Master Relaxation
children.top_down_role: Master representations providing poor bounds or weak discrimination among candidate decisions.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Master Relaxation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive-gap criterion for weakness of a decomposition master relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be the master domain, let \(c:X\to\mathbb{R}\), and let \(Q:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be the exact recourse value. Define \(z^*=\inf_{x\in X}\{c(x)+Q(x)\}\). A master relaxation \(R\subseteq X\times\mathbb{R}\) is valid when \((x,Q(x))\in R\) for every \(x\) with finite recourse, and its lower bound is \[L_R=\inf\{c(x)+\theta:(x,\theta)\in R\}.\] For a prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\), the relaxation is weak if \(z^*-L_R>\varepsilon\). For nested masters \(R_{k+1}\subseteq R_k\), persistent weakness means \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}(z^*-L_{R_k})>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid master relaxation is weak when its lower bound remains more than the prescribed tolerance below the true decomposed optimum.
assumptions_latex: \(X\neq\varnothing\) and \(z^*\in\mathbb{R}\).
Every master relaxation contains the exact recourse epigraph over finite-recourse decisions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weakness at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) is exactly the inequality \(z^*-L_R>\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Exact optimal value of the subproblem induced by x.
Feasible set of the relaxed master in decision–recourse-value space.

children.top_down_role: Master-side estimates that misrepresent subproblem contributions across related assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Inconsistent Recourse Estimation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency test for lower recourse estimators generated by accumulating master cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be the exact recourse function and let \(\underline Q_k:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\) be the estimator after iteration \(k\). For a master that permanently retains all valid recourse cuts, the estimator sequence is consistent precisely when \[\underline Q_k(x)\le Q(x)\quad\text{and}\quad \underline Q_{k+1}(x)\ge\underline Q_k(x)\] for every \(x\in X\) and every \(k\). Recourse estimation is inconsistent if either inequality fails: overestimation destroys lower-bound validity, while a decrease at a retained point contradicts monotonicity of an accumulating-cut master.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Accumulated lower recourse estimates are inconsistent if they ever exceed true recourse or decrease between iterations despite retaining every valid cut.
assumptions_latex: All recourse cuts retained through iteration \(k\) remain active at iteration \(k+1\).
Each \(\underline Q_k\) is intended to be a global lower estimator of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Inconsistency occurs iff some \((x,k)\) violates lower-bound validity or monotonicity.

notation.meaning: Master-side lower recourse estimator at iteration k.

children.title: Master Guidance Failure
children.top_down_role: Search behavior caused by unreliable ranking, bounding, or screening of master states.

knowledge_statements.title: Master Guidance Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Persistent selection of materially suboptimal decisions by a valid lower-estimating master.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=c(x)+Q(x)\), let \(z^*=\inf_{x\in X}F(x)\), and suppose the master selects \(x^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\{c(x)+\underline Q_k(x)\}\), where \(\underline Q_k(x)\le Q(x)\). Master guidance fails persistently if there exist \(\delta>0\) and an infinite index set \(K\) such that, for every \(k\in K\), \[F(x^k)-z^*\ge\delta\quad\text{and}\quad Q(x^k)-\underline Q_k(x^k)\ge\delta.\] Thus valid master bounds can coexist with repeated selection of decisions uniformly separated from optimality when their recourse is persistently underestimated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Guidance fails when a valid master repeatedly selects decisions bounded away from optimality because their recourse remains materially underestimated.
assumptions_latex: \(z^*\in\mathbb{R}\) and each displayed master minimum is attained.
The estimators satisfy \(\underline Q_k(x)\le Q(x)\) globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed uniform gaps characterize persistent master-guidance failure along \(K\).

notation.meaning: Recourse lower estimator used by the kth master.

children.title: Recourse Bound Reliability
children.top_down_role: Validity scope of lower or upper recourse estimates used by the master.

knowledge_statements.title: Recourse Bound Reliability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise certificate for trustworthy lower and upper recourse bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a master decision \(x\in X\). Let \(Y(x)\) be its subproblem feasible set, let \(q(x,\cdot):Y(x)\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and define \[Q(x)=\inf\{q(x,y):y\in Y(x)\},\] with \(Q(x)=+\infty\) when \(Y(x)=\varnothing\). A pair \((L(x),U(x))\in(\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\})\times(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\})\) is a reliable recourse-bound certificate when \[L(x)\le Q(x)\le U(x),\] the lower inequality is supported by a valid relaxation or dual certificate, and every finite upper bound has the form \(U(x)=q(x,\bar y)\) for a verifiably feasible \(\bar y\in Y(x)\). For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the certificate is \(\varepsilon\)-accurate when both bounds are finite and \(U(x)-L(x)\le\varepsilon\). If \(B\in\mathbb{R}\) is a certified incumbent upper bound for the minimization problem and \(L(x)\ge B\), then the fixed decision \(x\) cannot yield a strict incumbent improvement; a finite witnessed \(U(x)\) certifies attainable recourse at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reliable pointwise recourse bounds use a valid relaxation or dual certificate for the lower bound and a feasible subproblem witness for every finite upper bound. A lower bound no smaller than a certified incumbent value rules out a strict improvement at that fixed master decision.
assumptions_latex: The value \(q(x,\bar y)\) and the condition \(\bar y\in Y(x)\) are independently verifiable.
The lower-bound derivation applies to the exact subproblem at \(x\).
The incumbent threshold \(B\) is a certified upper bound for the minimization problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A finite certified interval contains \(Q(x)\); width at most \(\varepsilon\) certifies \(\varepsilon\)-accuracy, and \(L(x)\ge B\) excludes strict improvement at the fixed decision \(x\).

notation.meaning: Exact recourse infimum at the fixed master decision x.
Certified lower and upper recourse bounds.
Feasible subproblem witness supporting a finite upper bound.
Certified incumbent upper bound for the overall minimization problem.

children.title: Uncertified or Inexact Subproblem Reasoning
children.top_down_role: Subproblem outcomes that cannot support exact pruning, bounds, or finite-convergence claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Uncertified or Inexact Subproblem Reasoning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity boundary for pruning and cuts derived from approximate subproblem outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(x\in X\) and suppose a subproblem routine returns only \(\widehat Q(x)\), with neither a certified interval containing \(Q(x)\) nor a proof of infeasibility. For any \(\eta>0\), the observation is compatible with the alternative value \(Q(x)=\widehat Q(x)-\eta\) unless an error guarantee excludes it. Consequently, pruning from \(\widehat Q(x)\ge B\) is invalid whenever \(\widehat Q(x)-\eta<B\) remains possible, and an infeasibility cut is invalid without a verifiable contradiction certificate. Exact finite-convergence claims therefore cross their validity boundary when approximate subproblem outputs are used as exact bounds or feasibility decisions without certified errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate subproblem result cannot justify exact pruning, infeasibility cuts, or finite convergence unless certified bounds or contradiction evidence exclude adverse alternatives.
assumptions_latex: The routine supplies no independently verifiable error bound or infeasibility certificate.
The threshold \(B\in\mathbb{R}\) is used for a pruning decision.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uncertified \(\widehat Q(x)\) alone cannot establish \(Q(x)\ge B\) or subproblem infeasibility.
